<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_document">Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures<span class="ltx_pubnotes"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_thanks"><span class="ltx_note_name">Thanks: </span><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">We are grateful to Lin William Cong, Urban Jermann, Shimon Kogan, Stefan Nagel, Tim Roughgarden, Adrien Verdelhan, as well as conference participants at the 2024 Utah Winter Finance Conference and seminar participants at a16z Crypto, Bank of Israel, Hebrew University, Reichman University, the University of Chicago, and the Virtual Derivatives Workshop for their insightful feedback and helpful comments.
Songrun He is at Washington University in St. Louis (<a href="mailto:h.songrun@wustl.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">h.songrun@wustl.edu</a>). Asaf Manela is at Washington University in St. Louis and Reichman University (<a href="mailto:amanela@wustl.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">amanela@wustl.edu</a>). Omri Ross is at University of Copenhagen (<a href="mailto:omri@di.ku.dk" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">omri@di.ku.dk</a>), and Chief Blockchain Scientist at the eToro Group. Victor von Wachter is at University of Copenhagen (<a href="mailto:victor.vonwachter@di.ku.dk" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">victor.vonwachter@di.ku.dk</a>).</span></span></span></span></h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

<div class="ltx_dates">First draft December 2022. This draft September 2026.</div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract">
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures are the most popular cryptocurrency derivatives. Perpetuals offer leveraged exposure to their underlying without rollover or direct ownership. Unlike fixed-maturity futures, perpetuals are not guaranteed to converge to the spot price. To minimize the gap between perpetual and spot prices, long investors periodically pay shorts a funding rate proportional to this gap. We derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures in frictionless markets and bounds in markets with trading costs. Empirically, deviations from these prices in crypto are larger than in traditional currency markets, comove across currencies, and diminish over time. An implied arbitrage strategy yields high Sharpe ratios.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">JEL Classification</span>: G11, G12, G13 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Keywords</span>: Perpetual futures, crypto, random-maturity arbitrage, funding rate, clamp</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures are, by far, the most popular derivative traded in cryptocurrency markets, generating a daily volume of more than $100 billion.
Prior to the recent collapse of FTX, perpetual futures were among the most actively traded products on the exchange, with the now-bankrupt hedge fund Alameda Research taking the other side of many such leveraged trades. Despite their central role in crypto markets, and their potential adoption by traditional derivative markets, there is relatively little work studying these derivatives. In this paper we ask: what are the theoretical fundamental values of perpetual futures, and how large are deviations from these fundamentals empirically?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetuals are derivatives that allow investors to speculate on or hedge against cryptocurrency price fluctuations using high leverage, without needing to acquire the cryptocurrencies or to roll them over.
Like traditional fixed-maturity futures, at initiation, a long and short counterparty agree on an initial futures price without exchanging any money, other than posting margin with the exchange. Both parties can enter or exit the contract at any time, with profits or losses continuously calculated and allocated to each side’s margin account based on prevailing market prices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike fixed-maturity futures, perpetuals do not expire. This feature enhances the liquidity of the contract, as there is no staggering of contracts with different maturities traded on the exchange, and only a single perpetual futures contract per underlying asset is listed. Moreover, this instrument does not require market participants to roll over their futures positions and is traded 24/7.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Because they have no set expiration date, perpetuals are not guaranteed to converge to the spot price of their underlying asset at any given time, and the usual no-arbitrage prices for perpetuals are not applicable without additional restrictions.
To minimize the gap between perpetual futures and spot prices, long position holders periodically pay short position holders a ’funding rate’ proportional to this gap to incentivize trades that narrow it.
For example, when the futures price exceeds the spot price, arbitrageurs who borrow cash to long the spot and simultaneously short the futures would receive the funding rate. Their trades would tend to increase the spot price and decrease the futures price.
A narrow gap means that perpetual futures offer effective exposure to variation in the spot price of the underlying asset to hedging and speculating investors. Typically, the funding rate is paid every eight hours and approximately equals the average futures-spot spread over the preceding eight hours.
Note that the strategy just sketched, commonly referred to as ’funding rate arbitrage,’ is not risk-free even disregarding margin requirements and trading costs, simply because there is no predetermined expiration date when the trade would be unwound at a profit.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures in frictionless markets and derive no-arbitrage bounds in markets with trading costs.
The theoretical perpetual futures price is proportional to the spot price of the underlying, with a constant of proportionality determined by the interaction of interest rates and the exchange’s funding rate mechanism. A key feature of this mechanism is the ‘clamp’ - when futures and spot prices are close, the funding rate is fixed at a small positive value, but when they diverge significantly, the funding rate increases linearly with the price gap to incentivize convergence. The interest rate captures the cost of borrowing cash to finance holding the underlying, while the funding rate intensity captures the benefit of shorting the futures. Thus, intuitively, the futures-spot spread is larger when the cash borrowing interest rate is large relative to the funding rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our derivation relies on a generalized notion of arbitrage that we call <em id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">random-maturity arbitrage</em>. Unlike traditional riskless arbitrage, which fixes the liquidation date in advance, we allow the strategy to be unwound at a bounded stopping time determined by the evolution of prices.
At first glance, one might object that such prices are not truly based on riskless arbitrage. Note, however, that riskless no-arbitrage pricing is usually just a useful fiction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pedersen, 2019</a>)</cite>. In real-world futures markets, arbitrageurs must maintain a margin account during the entire period in which the arbitrage trade is open. Temporary worsening of apparent arbitrage opportunities can lead to liquidations and losses. As the saying goes, an arbitrageur must remain liquid longer than the market stays irrational. Thus, even arbitrage opportunities that appear to be riskless in theory may be risky in practice.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our no-arbitrage prices provide a useful benchmark for perpetual futures and simultaneously prescribe a strategy to exploit divergence from these fundamental values. Our analysis allows for jumps in both futures and spot prices.
Motivated by the theoretical understanding, we study the empirical deviations of the perpetual futures price from the spot. We find substantial and time-varying deviations, with perpetual futures trading above the no-arbitrage benchmark on average and converging to our suggested benchmark over time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Around this benchmark, however, perpetual futures often differ significantly from spot prices.
The mean <em id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">absolute</em> deviation is about 52% to 90% per year across different cryptocurrencies, which is considerably larger than the deviations documented in traditional currency markets by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018)</a></cite>.
We find strong comovement of the futures-spot gap across different cryptocurrencies. This comovement can be due to commonality in funding and market liquidity faced by arbitrageurs who operate in multiple cryptocurrencies. Common sentiment could also drive the difference in futures demand relative to the spot. Overall, the deviation’s magnitude is comparable to our theoretical no-arbitrage bound calibrated to actual trading fees.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Deviations decline on average about 22 percentage points a year, consistent with an increase in arbitrage capital and competition among arbitrageurs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kondor, 2009</a>)</cite>. The narrowing gap provides an additional perspective on the downfall of Alameda Research and Three Arrows Capital. According to news reports and interviews, both hedge funds seem to have pivoted from such arbitrage activity around late 2021 to early 2022 and started taking more directional bets on cryptocurrencies, with both direct unhedged crypto holdings and investments in crypto startups. The large declines in crypto prices in 2022 subsequently exhausted their capital and led to their bankruptcies.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          See, for example, Forbes, November 19, 2022, on <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/jeffkauflin/2022/11/19/how-did-sam-bankman-frieds-alameda-research-lose-so-much-money" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">How Did Sam Bankman-Fried’s Alameda Research Lose So Much Money?</a>, Odd Lots, November 17, 2022, on <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-17/odd-lots-podcast-understanding-sam-bankman-fried-s-ftx-crypto-collapse" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Understanding the Collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s Crypto Empire</a>, and Hugh Hendry’s interview on December 3, 2022 of Kyle Davies on the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TzGdkB0xbCE" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Collapse of Three Arrows Capital</a>.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">To understand the economics of the futures-spot spread, we consider a trading strategy motivated by the random-maturity arbitrage theory. Whenever the futures-spot spread exceeds the theoretical bound for a given trading cost tier, we open the trading position and close it when the futures-spot spread returns to its theoretical relationship under no trading costs. We find that empirically, the random maturity arbitrage strategy generates a sizable Sharpe ratio even under high trading costs. For example, for Bitcoin perpetual futures, the strategy generates a Sharpe ratio of 3.35 under high trading costs typical of retail investors, and up to 11.65 for highly active market makers who pay no such fees. After additionally accounting for effective bid-ask spreads, the corresponding Sharpe ratios remain 3.27 and 10.46. The strategy’s performance is even better for Ether and other cryptocurrencies and delivers significant alphas relative to the 3-factor model of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu, Tsyvinski, and Wu (2022)</a></cite> and the 5-factor model of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong, Karolyi, Tang, and Zhao (2022b)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">The strong performance of our simple trading strategy, which exploits deviations from the random-maturity no-arbitrage bounds we derive, provides compelling evidence for the usefulness of these bounds as a benchmark for perpetual futures prices. The strategy generates high Sharpe ratios, even for investors subject to the highest trading costs on Binance. This indicates that the no-arbitrage prices serve as an effective anchor for perpetual futures, with profitable random maturity arbitrage opportunities arising when market prices diverge significantly from these fundamental values. Thus, the success of the trading strategy underscores the practical value and validity of our theoretical no-arbitrage results.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">What explains these large no-arbitrage deviations? We organize the evidence with a simple model in which end users demand perpetual futures for leveraged exposure, while arbitrageurs take the other side and hedge in the spot market subject to trading costs and limited balance-sheet capacity. The model delivers two predictions. First, relaxing arbitrageurs’ capital constraints should compress futures-spot deviations. Second, end-user demand should have a larger price impact when arbitrage capacity is constrained.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Both predictions receive support in the data. We exploit Binance’s April 2022 introduction of portfolio margining, which allowed arbitrageurs to net collateral across their spot and futures positions and thereby increased the capital efficiency of the arbitrage trade. Deviations compress significantly following its introduction. We also find that perpetual-futures order flow has substantially greater price impact when initial deviations are large, when arbitrage capacity is more likely to bind. Together, these results point to limited arbitrage capacity as an important force behind the large deviations we document. Finally, we find that past returns positively predict futures-spot deviations. Following high spot returns, perpetual futures tend to trade at higher prices relative to the no-arbitrage benchmark, consistent with extrapolative demand for leveraged perpetual exposure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p14.1" class="ltx_p">The existing literature on perpetual futures mainly focuses on empirical evidence. See e.g. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alexander, Choi, Park, and Sohn (2020)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">De Blasis and Webb (2022)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferko, Moin, Onur, and Penick (2022)</a></cite>, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Streltsov and Ruan (2022)</a></cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christin, Routledge, Soska, and Zetlin-Jones (2022)</a></cite> present a novel study on the strategy of longing the spot and shorting the perpetual futures to understand the demand pressure in the market. They document a significant return to this trading strategy and attribute the profits to differences of opinion and leverage constraints in the market. We find that our dynamic real-time trading strategy outperforms their directional bet even under a high trading cost scenario. Our paper provides a general explanation for their findings as perpetual futures are more expensive relative to the theoretical no-arbitrage price for most of the recent sample period across major cryptocurrencies. Therefore, longing the spot and shorting the futures would be consistent with arbitrage trading directions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p15.1" class="ltx_p">On the theory side, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angeris, Chitra, Evans, and Lorig (2022)</a></cite> provide a theoretical no-arbitrage analysis of perpetuals, which relies on a strong assumption that the payoff from the perpetual is a fixed function of the underlying spot price and focuses on the security design problem. Their approach would not be able to analyze arbitrage trading in case of a deviation from the no-arbitrage price. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ackerer et al. (2023)</a></cite> derive no-arbitrage prices for various perpetual contracts in both discrete and continuous-time by assuming the existence of an equivalent martingale measure. Our work advances this literature in three key ways: First, we derive no-arbitrage prices that incorporate realistic funding specifications, including the clamp feature used by major exchanges like Binance. Second, we provide explicit arbitrage bounds and trading strategies for markets with transaction costs. Third, we demonstrate empirically that our benchmark improves arbitrage strategy performance compared to existing approaches. We further relate our work to both papers below.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p16.1" class="ltx_p">Also related is a recent literature on fixed maturity futures in the crypto market. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmeling, Schrimpf, and Todorov (2022)</a></cite> provide a comprehensive analysis of the carry of fixed-maturity crypto futures, with the carry defined following the general definition of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen, and Vrugt (2018)</a></cite>. They document volatile convenience yields for fixed-maturity crypto futures and attribute this to trend-chasing small investors and the relative scarcity of arbitrage capital. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong, He, and Tang (2022a)</a></cite> provide a novel link between the volatile convenience yield and staking, service flow, and transaction convenience of the underlying tokens. They show that the large deviation from uncovered interest rate parity can be reconciled with transaction convenience. Our paper focuses on perpetual futures rather than fixed maturity futures and extends fixed-maturity to random-maturity no-arbitrage pricing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p17" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p17.1" class="ltx_p">More broadly, our paper contributes to the understanding of frictions and arbitrage in cryptocurrency markets. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Makarov and Schoar (2020)</a></cite> study price deviations across exchanges. They find large gaps across countries, highlighting the important role played by capital controls and slow-moving arbitrage capital as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duffie (2010)</a></cite>. Our analysis focuses on the price wedge between the spot and the futures market. We find that even within an exchange, futures prices deviate from their theoretical arbitrage-free values. These results indicate there are significant limits to arbitrage as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gromb and Vayanos (2018)</a></cite> for cryptocurrencies in the early years. Finally, our finding that deviations from the no-arbitrage benchmark in crypto markets are highly correlated across currencies suggests that a common risk factor drives this variation as documented by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lustig, Roussanov, and Verdelhan (2011)</a></cite> in traditional currency markets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p18" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p18.1" class="ltx_p">The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section <a href="#S2" title="2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> provides the institutional details and history of perpetual futures. Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the no-arbitrage analysis of the perpetual futures market and derives the theoretical price of perpetual futures. Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> demonstrates the empirical futures-spot deviation, implements the theory-motivated arbitrage strategy, and examines execution costs and liquidation risk.
Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> studies the economic mechanism behind the deviations and tests predictions concerning arbitrage capacity and the price impact of end-user demand.
Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Conclusion ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> concludes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>An Introduction to Perpetual Futures</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The idea of perpetual futures was first introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shiller (1993)</a></cite>. The goal was to set up a perpetual claim on the cash flows of an illiquid asset. For example, the underlying illiquid asset could be a house that generates rents as cash flows. The purpose of perpetual futures is to enable price discovery for the underlying with an illiquid or hard-to-measure price. Perpetual futures have no expiration date but cash is exchanged between the long and the short side: after buying the perpetual futures, the long side is entitled to receive the cash flow from the short side and they settle the price difference when exiting the position.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v7/figures/exchange_volume.png" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/184;" width="476" height="184" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Total trading volumes of perpetual futures across exchanges</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S2.F1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The figure displays the 7-day moving average daily traded volume for perpetual futures across all exchanges in blue. The median daily volume is $17.8 bn. (2020), $132.0 bn. (2021) and $101.9 bn. (2022). This translates to a yearly volume of $8,551 bn. (2020), $51,989 bn. (2021) and $39,306 bn. (2022) respectively. Additionally, the grey line depicts the ratio between the traded volume in perpetuals and spot markets. In 2022, perpetual futures markets consistently traded between 2x and 3.5x spot volume. The data is obtained from CoinGecko, a crypto data specialist. We exclude exchanges that are known for misrepresenting data (e.g., forms of wash trading).</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures in crypto markets similarly have no expiration date and cash is exchanged between the long and the short side, but their purpose is different from Shiller’s original idea. First, unlike, e.g., the real estate market, crypto has no inherent dividend or cash flow. Second, the price discovery argument of Shiller is most applicable to settings where spot prices are difficult to measure. Crypto spot prices, however, can be measured from active trading on different exchanges, and decentralized exchanges such as Bancor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hertzog et al., 2017</a>)</cite> or Uniswap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Adams et al., 2021</a>)</cite> offer price discovery for assets with minimal liquidity. The major role perpetual futures play in the crypto space is to offer an effective leveraged trading vehicle to hedge against or speculate on the underlying spot price movement, which makes the market more complete. Perpetual futures can also facilitate tax management. For example, an investor holding an appreciated token can reduce or hedge the associated price exposure by taking an offsetting perpetual futures position rather than selling the underlying token. In jurisdictions where capital gains on the token are recognized upon disposition, this may allow investors to defer realization of the embedded capital gain while retaining the underlying position.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Crypto perpetual futures were first introduced by BitMEX in 2016, which have gained great popularity in the crypto space since their inception. It initially served as an effective hedging tool for crypto miners. It was later adopted by crypto speculators interested in leveraged exposure.
Nowadays, based on data from CoinGecko, the median total daily trading volume of perpetual futures across all exchanges is 101.9 billion in the year 2022 which is about <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times</annotation></semantics></math> the total spot trading volume across these exchanges. Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> presents the 7-day moving average of the total trading volume of perpetual futures across all exchanges. We see a significant rise in trading of perpetual futures around January 2021 and the total volume stabilizes at a level above $100 billion per day following the rise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">More recently, decentralized perpetual futures venues have emerged as significant competitors to centralized exchanges. A prominent example is Hyperliquid<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs</a>.</span></span></span>, a high-performance decentralized exchange built on its own Layer 1 blockchain with a fully on-chain order book. Launched in 2023 in the wake of the FTX collapse, Hyperliquid aims to combine the speed and usability of centralized venues with the transparency of decentralized finance. Its rapid growth in trading volume, including its ability to process large-scale liquidations during the October 2025 crypto flash crash, illustrates a broader trend toward on-chain derivatives infrastructure that could reshape the competitive landscape of perpetual futures markets. The contract specification on Hyperliquid mirrors that of Binance, including the clamp feature. Our theoretical results, therefore, apply directly to this exchange as well.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong, Li, Tang, and Yang (2022c)</a></cite> document significant wash trading behavior among crypto exchanges because of competition, the ranking mechanism, and lack of regulation. They estimate that over 70% of crypto trading volume is not real. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amiram, Lyandres, and Rabetti (2021)</a></cite> confirm this conclusion using new data and an extended methodology. Therefore, in calculating trading volume, we exclude exchanges that are known to misrepresent data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v7/figures/exchanges_fr_bitcoin.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/192;" width="476" height="192" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Bitcoin annualized funding rate across exchanges</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.F2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S2.F2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The figure presents the 7-day moving average annualized funding rate for Bitcoin (BTC) across exchanges. The data is obtained from Glassnode, an analytics platform. The data covers two major market turbulences: the COVID stock market crash from February to April 2020 and the FTX insolvency in November 2022. The FTX collapse led to significant negative funding rates on all solvent exchanges. Thus, the perpetual futures prices were lower than the spot prices on the solvent exchanges. Vice versa on the insolvent FTX. The funding rates become more volatile after the event, indicating increased uncertainty for the market participants.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">A key feature of crypto perpetual futures is the funding rate, which is the cash exchanged between the long and short counterparties. Its goal is to keep the futures price close to the underlying spot so that the futures can be an effective hedging tool for spot price movement. The funding rate is typically paid every 8 hours. Its value is approximately a weighted average of the prior 8 hours’ price gap of the futures and the spot. If the futures price is above the spot, the funding rate will be positive, meaning the long side of the futures needs to pay the short side. This incentivizes traders to short the futures, and in doing so, to move its price back in line with the spot. On the other hand, when the futures price is below the spot, the funding rate turns negative, which means the short side needs to pay the long side. Therefore, the funding rate is the key mechanism keeping the futures price close to the spot price.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031</a> provides a detailed explanation of how the funding rate is calculated. We summarize the mechanism in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Funding Rate Calculation on Binance ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</span></span></span> Note that perpetual futures cannot be replicated by rolling over 8-hour maturity futures. For the latter, every 8 hours, the price is guaranteed to converge to the underlying spot, while for the perpetual futures this is not the case.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> presents the annualized 7-day moving average of Bitcoin perpetual funding rates across leading exchanges from January 2020 to December 2022.
The funding rate is positive when the futures-to-spot spread is positive, and negative otherwise. Funding rates tend to be similar across exchanges due to cross-exchange arbitrage activity, but can diverge during extreme liquidity episodes. During March 2020, as COVID-19 started to spread and liquidity evaporated, funding rates turned substantially negative in most exchanges. Funding rates turned highly positive during the crypto bull run of early 2021. The last episode highlighted is the collapse of FTX, which was the 4th largest crypto exchange at the time. The figure shows that Bitcoin futures prices were substantially higher than spot prices at FTX, but the opposite was true on other exchanges. This pattern is consistent with FTX investors liquidating their short futures positions quickly, either voluntarily to reduce their exposure to the failing exchange, or involuntarily as the exchange liquidated their underfunded positions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Two forces account for the remaining dispersion in funding rates in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. First, there are segmentations in arbitrage across exchanges because exchanges do not offer cross-margining across venues. An arbitrageur exploiting a funding-rate differential must therefore fund and margin the two legs separately, tying up capital on each exchange and limiting the amount of arbitrage capital that can respond to a given discrepancy. Second, exchanges differ substantially in liquidity. From 2020 to 2022, Binance accounts for approximately 49% of Bitcoin perpetual trading volume across the five exchanges in the figure, compared with only 0.2% for Bitfinex. Funding rates on a relatively illiquid venue such as Bitfinex can therefore be more sensitive to exchange-specific order flow and trading conditions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The comparison between Binance and Bybit can further illustrate this mechanism. Their funding rates are highly correlated, at 0.74, consistent with active cross-exchange arbitrage, yet meaningful divergences remain during periods of unusually large funding payments. We apply the effective spread estimator of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Roll (1984)</a></cite> to trade-level data from the two venues and find that the effective spread of the Bitcoin perpetual on Bybit exceeds that on Binance on every day in our sampled subset, by a factor ranging from two to ten.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
            
            
            
          We sample seven days spanning the episodes in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, using the trade-by-trade archives that Binance and Bybit publish for the BTC perpetual.</span></span></span> Because of the differences in liquidity and arbitrage capital, the same order flow can move the perpetual futures price further on Bybit compared to Binance. Thus, although arbitrage keeps prices and funding rates closely linked across exchanges in normal times, it does not eliminate venue-specific deviations. When liquidity is thinner, and arbitrage capital is more constrained, a given imbalance in demand can generate a larger price response and, consequently, a larger funding-rate differential.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, the residual cross-exchange dispersion in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reflects the limits of arbitrage across segmented trading venues, which can be a promising avenue for future research.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures relative to spot prices. Unlike traditional futures, perpetual futures have no expiration date. To analyze arbitrage in this market, we generalize the traditional notion of risk-free arbitrage, where arbitrageurs have a guaranteed positive payoff at a certain time in the future. We first describe the payoff structure of perpetual futures. We then introduce a generalized notion of an arbitrage opportunity with a certain positive payoff but at an uncertain future time.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Perpetual futures)<span id="Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A perpetual futures contract with price <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> written on an underlying asset with spot price <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> is a swap agreement between the long and the short side. Define the premium index at time <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s}\equiv\frac{F_{s}-S_{s}}{F_{s}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>≡</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s}\equiv\frac{F_{s}-S_{s}}{F_{s}}.</annotation></semantics></math> There is no exchange of principal to open the position. Once open, both the long side and the short side can terminate their position at any time <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. To stay in the contract, both sides have to meet two requirements. (1) For each unit of the perpetual, the long and short sides must exchange an <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{s}-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{s}-</annotation></semantics></math>adapted cash flow <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(p_{s})F_{s}ds," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(p_{s})F_{s}ds,</annotation></semantics></math> referred to as the funding payment, at each time <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\in(0,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\in(0,t)</annotation></semantics></math>. The funding rate function <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(\cdot):\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(\cdot):\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is a univariate function of the premium index. If <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(p_{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(p_{s})</annotation></semantics></math> is positive, the long pays the short, and vice versa. (2) Both sides need to post mark-to-market margins to cover any losses in their margin accounts.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\{\mathcal{F}_{t}\}_{t\geq 0},\mathbb{P})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>ℙ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\{\mathcal{F}_{t}\}_{t\geq 0},\mathbb{P})</annotation></semantics></math> be a
filtered probability space, where <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the information available
to the arbitrageur at time <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. The traditional notions of arbitrage typically consider a guaranteed positive payoff at a certain future date. For example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cochrane (2009)</a></cite> defines arbitrage as follows. Let <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the net payoff from a trading strategy if all positions are liquidated at time <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 2</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Riskless Arbitrage)<span id="Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A riskless arbitrage is a trading strategy with nonpositive initial cost and a
deterministic future time <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T&lt;\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T&lt;\infty</annotation></semantics></math> such that
(1) <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{T}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{T}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely and
(2) <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pr(X_{T}&gt;0)&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pr(X_{T}&gt;0)&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">There is no certain future time, however, when a perpetual futures contract expires, and its price is guaranteed to converge to some fixed function of the spot price. Therefore, a generalized notion of arbitrage is required. We define <em id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">random-maturity arbitrage</em> opportunities as zero-cost strategies with a guaranteed positive payoff at a bounded uncertain future time. Stated formally:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 3</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Random-maturity arbitrage)<span id="Thmtheorem3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A random-maturity arbitrage is a trading strategy with nonpositive initial cost together
with an <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathcal{F}_{t}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathcal{F}_{t}\}</annotation></semantics></math>-stopping time <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> such that, for some deterministic
<math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{T}&lt;\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>&lt;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{T}&lt;\infty</annotation></semantics></math>,
(1) <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\leq\bar{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\leq\bar{T}</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely,
(2) <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{\tau}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{\tau}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely, and
(3) <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pr(X_{\tau}&gt;0)&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>τ</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pr(X_{\tau}&gt;0)&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Definition <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Definition 3 (Random-maturity arbitrage). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> generalizes traditional arbitrage in the sense that there is a guaranteed positive payoff but at an uncertain future time. Because <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is a stopping time, the decision to unwind at time <math id="S3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> can depend only on information available up to time <math id="S3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. Riskless arbitrage is the special case in which <math id="S3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\equiv T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>≡</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\equiv T</annotation></semantics></math> is deterministic. The following corollary specializes this definition for perpetual futures:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmcorollary1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_corollary">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmcorollary1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 1</span></span><span id="Thmcorollary1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmcorollary1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmcorollary1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmcorollary1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">In the perpetual futures market, if a strategy (1) has <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> cost at time <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>, and (2) for any price path of the futures and the spot, <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists a bounded unwinding time <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> such that the strategy’s discounted payoff is positive, then this strategy is a random-maturity arbitrage.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Throughout our no-arbitrage analysis, we abstract from exchange default risk and assume that the exchange remains solvent. If the exchange can default before the unwinding stopping time, funding payments, gains on the futures position, or posted collateral may not be fully recovered. The convergence strategy would then no longer have a guaranteed nonnegative payoff and therefore need not constitute a random-maturity arbitrage under our definition. Thus, our no-arbitrage results should be interpreted as conditional on exchange solvency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our analysis is quite general and allows for jumps in both futures and spot prices. We next show that when there is no random-maturity arbitrage, the futures price is a fixed constant times the spot price. First, we state three key assumptions needed for our results:<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
            
            
            
          For a function <math id="footnote5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>, we define its generalized (set-valued) inverse as: <math id="footnote5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{-1}(y)=\{x:f(x)=y\}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{-1}(y)=\{x:f(x)=y\}.</annotation></semantics></math></span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 1</span></span><span id="Thmassumption1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The risk-free short rate <math id="Thmassumption1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> in the cash market is constant.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 2</span></span><span id="Thmassumption2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The ratio between the price of perpetual futures and the spot is bounded: <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0&lt;\underline{R}\leq\frac{F_{t}(\omega)}{S_{t}(\omega)}\leq\overline{R}&lt;\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&lt;</mo><munder accentunder="true"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo>&lt;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0&lt;\underline{R}\leq\frac{F_{t}(\omega)}{S_{t}(\omega)}\leq\overline{R}&lt;\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall t,\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>ω</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall t,\omega</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 3</span></span><span id="Thmassumption3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The funding rate function <math id="Thmassumption3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is weakly increasing in its argument, and its level set at the risk-free rate, <math id="Thmassumption3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi^{-1}(r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi^{-1}(r)</annotation></semantics></math>, is a nonempty compact interval <math id="Thmassumption3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[x_{-},x_{+}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[x_{-},x_{+}]</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="Thmassumption3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{+}&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{+}&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> guarantees that there is no roll-over risk for the arbitrageurs. In Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Stochastic Interest Rates ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>, we relax this assumption and show that stochastic short rates leave the structure of the arbitrage payoff intact up to an empirically small rebalancing term. Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> says that the ratio between the perpetual futures price and the spot price is bounded away from zero and infinity. Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption3" title="Assumption 3. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> states that the design of the contract needs to guarantee that there is a reward for convergence trade. The reward should be weakly increasing when the deviation becomes larger. The condition that <math id="S3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi^{-1}(r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi^{-1}(r)</annotation></semantics></math> is a nonempty compact interval ensures that the funding rate reaches the risk-free rate over a well-defined range of deviations, while <math id="S3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{+}&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{+}&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math> ensures that the corresponding equilibrium futures price is positive. With these three assumptions, we can state our result as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmproposition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmproposition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 1</span></span><span id="Thmproposition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(No-arbitrage price: General Case)<span id="Thmproposition1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmproposition1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproposition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproposition1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Suppose <math id="Thmproposition1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi^{-1}(r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi^{-1}(r)</annotation></semantics></math> is a single point. Under Assumptions <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, and <a href="#Thmassumption3" title="Assumption 3. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, there is an absence of random-maturity arbitrage opportunities if and only if</span></p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}=(1-\Phi^{-1}(r))^{-1}S_{t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}=(1-\Phi^{-1}(r))^{-1}S_{t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text">The proof is provided in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Proofs ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">We next provide the economic intuition behind Proposition <a href="#Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price: General Case). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and derive the payoff expressions that we use below. Start off with the conjecture that in equilibrium, the futures price is a linear function of the spot, <math id="S3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}=\lambda S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}=\lambda S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, for some constant <math id="S3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>. If this conjecture is true, it implies both arbitrage strategies laid out in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> should always have <math id="S3.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> payoff.</p>
</div>

From the second equality, we obtain the key condition for pinning down the value of <math id="S3.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>

<p id="S3.p10.3" class="ltx_p">which states that in equilibrium, the funding rate must equal the risk-free rate. When <math id="S3.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi^{-1}(r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi^{-1}(r)</annotation></semantics></math> can be mapped to a single point, it pins down the equilibrium <math id="S3.p10.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>

<p id="S3.p10.4" class="ltx_p">Thus, <math id="S3.p10.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> depends on the risk-free rate <math id="S3.p10.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>. Under Assumption
<a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <math id="S3.p10.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is constant, so <math id="S3.p10.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda(r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda(r)</annotation></semantics></math> is constant over time; for
notational simplicity, we henceforth write <math id="S3.p10.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda\equiv\lambda(r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda\equiv\lambda(r)</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, the relationship between F and S is exactly the one given in Equation (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price: General Case). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p11.1" class="ltx_p">If Equation (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price: General Case). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) always holds, then both strategies in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> have zero payoff forever. Indeed, in this case the perpetual futures is redundant given the spot and cash markets. Since the spot and cash markets admit no arbitrage, adding the perpetual futures cannot create a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Next, consider a deviation from this benchmark, where <math id="S3.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> (the opposite case has similar intuition). In this case, we consider the first strategy in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
For a fixed position in the convergence trade not to be an arbitrage opportunity, it must be that for all times <math id="S3.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> it does not generate a positive payoff by time <math id="S3.p12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, which requires that:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
