<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p12.2" class="ltx_p">Our proof shows that this cannot occur under the maintained assumptions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p13.1" class="ltx_p">To gain an intuition for these results, consider the three terms of Equation (<a href="#S3.E5" title="In 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). The first term is the initial spread. The second term is the present value of cumulated funding payments from initiation to unwinding. These first two terms account for gains to the arbitrageur in this scenario. The last term is the spread at unwinding discounted to the present, which is the source of tension here. For fixed-maturity futures, this spread is guaranteed to be zero at expiration. However, an arbitrageur in perpetual futures faces the risk that when they wish to unwind the trade, the spread may be large.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p14.1" class="ltx_p">Our key insight is that a positive and even modestly large spread can still leave the arbitrageur with a positive payoff because funding payments also increase with the spread. As long as the spread does not diverge to infinity, there will be some future bounded unwinding time <math id="S3.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> when the accumulated funding rate payments overcome any finite potential losses at unwinding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p15.1" class="ltx_p">Note that if we relax the assumption that the short rate is constant for arbitrageurs, this may introduce an additional risk to four parts in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>: (1) mark-to-market changes in futures price, (2) funding-rate payment, (3) reinvestment in the spot market, and (4) rollover of the short-term debt. In Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Stochastic Interest Rates ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>, we show that a stochastic short rate changes the payoff to the arbitrage strategies by a single additional term, a small rebalancing cash flow that accrues as the hedge ratio tracks the interest rate, and widens the no-arbitrage bound of Proposition <a href="#Thmproposition3" title="Proposition 3 (No-arbitrage bounds with trading costs). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> accordingly. This extension relates to the literature examining the differences between futures and forwards in the context of stochastic interest rates, such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cox et al. (1981)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grinblatt and Jegadeesh (1996)</a></cite>. They show that marking-to-market introduces an additional term in the futures price related to the covariance between the underlying asset and interest rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p16.1" class="ltx_p">Empirically, however, the interest rate changes required to rationalize the deviations we document are one to two orders of magnitude larger than observed movements in financing rates. Moreover, Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Stochastic Interest Rates ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> further shows that the additional payoff exposure generated by stochastic rates is a small rebalancing cash flow arising as the hedge ratio adjusts with the short rate.
Thus, stochastic interest rate risk is unlikely to account for the deviations we observe.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p17" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p17.1" class="ltx_p">For completeness, we next consider the edge case where for a given interest rate, the inverse of the funding rate function maps to an interval rather than a point. From Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we can see that this can happen on Binance if the interest rate exactly equals <math id="S3.p17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\iota" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ι</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\iota</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmproposition2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmproposition2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 2</span></span><span id="Thmproposition2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(No-arbitrage price: Edge Case)<span id="Thmproposition2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmproposition2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproposition2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproposition2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Suppose <math id="Thmproposition2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi^{-1}(r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi^{-1}(r)</annotation></semantics></math> is an interval. Under Assumptions <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, and <a href="#Thmassumption3" title="Assumption 3. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, there is an absence of random-maturity arbitrage opportunities if and only if</span></p>

</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.3" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.p18" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p18.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p18.1.1" class="ltx_text">The proof is provided in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Proofs ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p19" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p19.1" class="ltx_p">Having derived no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures for a general specification of the funding rate function <math id="S3.p19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math>, we next specialize these results for the case of Binance, which is currently the largest perpetual futures exchange by volume and the source of our data below.</p>
</div>

<div id="S3.4" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.p21" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p21.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p21.1.1" class="ltx_text">The proof follows from applying Propositions <a href="#Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price: General Case). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#Thmproposition2" title="Proposition 2 (No-arbitrage price: Edge Case). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> to the Binance funding rate function. We provide detailed scenario analysis in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Proofs ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>, which also gives the divergence speed of the deviation in this specific case.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p22" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p22.1" class="ltx_p">Empirically, the arbitrageurs face trading costs when opening or terminating their positions. Suppose they face a round-trip trading cost of <math id="S3.p22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>. We can derive no-arbitrage bounds for perpetual futures.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmproposition3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmproposition3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 3</span></span><span id="Thmproposition3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(No-arbitrage bounds with trading costs)<span id="Thmproposition3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmproposition3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproposition3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproposition3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under Assumptions <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, and <a href="#Thmassumption3" title="Assumption 3. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, and write</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

</div>
<div id="S3.p25" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p25.1" class="ltx_p">In the presence of trading costs, when the deviation of the perpetual futures price from <math id="S3.p25.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is larger than the round-trip trading costs <math id="S3.p25.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, arbitrageurs would have a strong incentive to trade perpetual futures toward the price <math id="S3.p25.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Proposition <a href="#Thmproposition3" title="Proposition 3 (No-arbitrage bounds with trading costs). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> also prescribes a trading strategy to exploit the futures-spot divergence in markets with different levels of trading costs. In the next section, we provide an empirical analysis of the futures-spot deviation and present arbitrage trading strategies motivated by our theory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p26" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p26.1" class="ltx_p">Before turning to the data, we pause to relate our results to two recent theoretical contributions.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angeris et al. (2022)</a></cite> consider an inverse problem to our setting. It assumes there is no arbitrage and that the perpetual futures price is a function of the spot, and derives the funding rate process that is consistent with the pricing formula. This takes a perspective of security design. However, empirically, funding rate mechanisms are predetermined and fixed for traders. Moreover, because of the limits of arbitrage, futures prices can deviate from the fixed function set by the designer. Our approach prescribes a strategy to exploit divergence from the fundamental price and offers a closer alignment with real-world trading conditions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p27" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p27.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ackerer et al. (2023)</a></cite>, our initial draft, disseminated December 2022 (see <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.06888v1" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.06888v1</a>), considers the case where the funding rate is a linear function of the premium index, as illustrated by the dashed line in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. It shows that the absence of random-maturity arbitrage opportunities implies the price of perpetual futures lies within the following bound relative to the spot:</p>
<table id="S3.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.p28" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p28.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ackerer et al. (2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11771v1)</a></cite>, dated October 2023, use a different set of assumptions and solution method to derive no-arbitrage prices for a class of perpetual contracts. In their paper, the price relevant for the case we analyzed is:</p>
<table id="S3.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<p id="S3.p28.2" class="ltx_p">Their paper further pointed out an inconsistency in the cash flow specification in our original derivation. After correcting this issue, Equation (<a href="#S3.E15" title="In 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>) above is consistent with their derivation in this case, and they deserve credit for deriving the correct formula first.<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
            
            
            
          We thank Damien Ackerer, Julien Hugonnier, and Urban Jermann for the comments that helped clarify the issue.</span></span></span> However, their framework does not allow for the clamp feature, an empirically important component of the funding rate specifications employed by major perpetual futures exchanges.<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
            
            
            
          According to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han (2024)</a></cite>, the exchanges which have perpetual futures with the clamp feature account for more than 75% of open interest for Bitcoin perpetual futures.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p29" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p29.1" class="ltx_p">Another advantage of our derivation is that it makes explicit the arbitrage trading strategy in case of deviations and provides bounds in the case of trading costs which we use in our empirical analysis. The approach also enables the analysis of no-arbitrage trading for the clamped funding rate, a specification less understood by practitioners so far according to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han (2024)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p30" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p30.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we differ in our assumptions about price deviations. We assume that the <em id="S3.p30.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">ratio</em> between the futures and spot is bounded, whereas <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ackerer et al. (2023)</a></cite> assume that a transversality condition holds such that the futures price (and therefore the spot) grows at a slow enough rate relative to the funding payments intensity <math id="S3.p30.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>. But even under their assumptions, it can be shown that strategies aimed at arbitrage of deviations from their benchmark prices are necessarily random-maturity arbitrage strategies, as we emphasize here.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p31" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p31.1" class="ltx_p">These pricing formulas imply different predictions for the point toward which the futures-spot basis should converge. In Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>, we directly compare these convergence targets in the data.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Data and Empirical Analysis</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct an empirical analysis of perpetual futures arbitrage strategies. We first describe the data and measure the deviations of the crypto futures-spot spread from the no-arbitrage benchmark. We then implement a trading strategy that exploits deviations from random-maturity no-arbitrage bounds. Finally, we examine implementation frictions by incorporating exchange fees and effective bid-ask spreads and assessing the interim losses relevant for liquidation risk.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Data</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We focus on the five largest cryptocurrencies excluding stablecoins: Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH), BNB (BNB), Dogecoin (DOGE), and Cardano (ADA) with a total market cap of $1.83 trillion, which account for 73.2% of the total market share of the Crypto market by March 2024.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each token, we obtain perpetual futures and spot prices at a 1-hour frequency from Binance. Binance is by far the leading exchange in the crypto realm: it accounts for about half of the perpetual futures volume of the exchanges in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and for the largest share of spot trading volume, and, as discussed in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, its perpetuals are also more liquid than those of the smaller venues in the figure. Another major benefit of using the Binance data is that every part of our trading strategies can be completed within the same platform without delay in transferring funds. As such, it approximates the real-world investment opportunities faced by traders.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We retrieve the perpetual funding rates from Binance, where the funding rate is paid every 8 hours. So we have futures and spot prices every hour and realized funding rate payments at 8:00, 16:00, and 0:00 GMT each day. The perpetual and spot tradings occur 24 hours per day and 7 days a week so there are no after-market hours.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> lists the starting and ending dates of our data for each cryptocurrency. Our data ends on 2024-03-11, covering the FTX fallout.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">

<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We obtain trading costs from Binance’s website<span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading</a> provides data on trading fees in perpetual futures and the spot market</span></span></span>. In general, trading costs for the spot market are significantly higher than those for perpetual futures for similar trading volume because futures are typically traded with leverage. Fee tiers are attributed to the 30-day trading volume. We attribute high trading costs with a 30-day spot trading volume above $1 million and futures trading volume above $15 million (small individual trader). Medium trading costs are attributed to a 30-day spot trading volume above $150 million and futures trading volume above $1 billion (small funds). Low trading costs are attributed to a 30-day spot trading volume above $2 billion and futures trading volume above 12.5 billion (large funds). Zero fees can be negotiated with customized contracts, for example, for market makers. We consider trading costs for makers instead of takers because institutions typically trade maker orders.<span id="footnote9" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">9</span>
              
              
              
            Takers trade market orders while makers trade limit orders. Takers take liquidity from the market while makers make the market or provide liquidity to the market.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Throughout our empirical analysis, <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the annualized interest-rate wedge that would rationalize the observed futures-spot spread. We denote its lower and upper no-arbitrage bounds implied by different tiers of trading costs by <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively. Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> formally defines <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and derives these bounds.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the specification of different trading costs. It also shows the random-maturity arbitrage bound for the deviation between the perpetual futures and the no-arbitrage price (<math id="S4.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>). The bounds become wider as the trading costs increase. Detailed explanations of the trading costs specifications are also provided in Appendix Figure <a href="#A1.F2" title="Figure A.2 ‣ Appendix A Additional Figures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a> and Figure <a href="#A1.F3" title="Figure A.3 ‣ Appendix A Additional Figures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Exchange Fee Tiers</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fee tiers are assigned based on past 30-day trading volume. The Spot and Futures columns report one-way maker trading fees, denoted
<math id="S4.T3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{S}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{F}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively, for a single transaction, expressed as a percentage of traded notional. The corresponding proportional round-trip cost of the two-legged arbitrage strategy is <math id="S4.T3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=2(c_{S}+c_{F})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>F</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=2(c_{S}+c_{F})</annotation></semantics></math>. High fees correspond to a 30-day trading volume above $1mn in spot and above $15mn in perpetuals, typically an individual trader. Medium fees apply to traders with 30-day trading volumes above $150mn in spot and above $1bn in perpetuals (small funds). Low fees are attributed to a 30-day trading volume above $2bn in spot and above $12.5bn in perpetuals (large funds). The no-fee tier can be negotiated with customized contracts, for example, for market makers. The <math id="S4.T3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math> columns report the theory-implied lower and upper no-arbitrage bounds for <math id="S4.T3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively, expressed in annualized percentage points and calculated using Equation (<a href="#S4.E19" title="In 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>).</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the direct trading fees, traders also face bid-ask spread and price impact costs in our arbitrage strategies. To assess the importance of such indirect trading costs, we obtain from Kaiko a high-frequency sample with one month of order book snapshots taken every 30 seconds. With this data, we estimate that the average bid-ask spread for perpetual futures is less than 0.05 bps, and the price impact of a trade with a size equal to 0.5 million is less than 0.3 bps. Combined, these indirect costs are less than 0.35 bps, which is substantially smaller than our direct trading fees. To study how trading costs evolve over the full sample, Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Effective Bid-Ask Spreads and the Cost of Arbitrage ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a> uses Binance’s public trade records to construct daily effective bid-ask spreads and incorporates them into the random-maturity arbitrage strategy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">To measure the deviation from the no-arbitrage price, we also obtain the interest rate data from Aave, a leading open-source DeFi liquidity protocol. Customers on Aave can either be suppliers or borrowers of cryptocurrencies. Because of the anonymity and decentralization of the DeFi system, all borrowings are over-collateralized and the collateral can serve as an additional supply to the system for borrowing. The customers can also supply spare currencies to the system to earn an interest rate. The supply interest rate is typically different from the borrowing interest rate. Both interest rates and their wedge are determined algorithmically based on the market conditions of supply and demand. We use interest rates from this platform because we believe it is a good proxy for the funding condition in the crypto market. Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Robustness to Alternative Risk-free Rate Measures ‣ Appendix D Additional Empirical Results ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a> shows that our results are robust to using the interest rate from the traditional financial market or using the margin borrowing rate from Binance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Our theory indicates using a risk-free rate available to the arbitrageurs. Therefore, we consider the interest rates on the stablecoins, which are not subject to volatile spot price movements and are the currency of denomination for perpetual futures margins. There are three major stablecoins traded on Aave: USDT, USDC, and DAI. To get a robust measure of the risk-free rate, we take an average of the three interest rates to arrive at our final risk-free supply and borrowing rate for the arbitrageurs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">We plot the time-series evolution of the interest rate in Appendix Figure <a href="#A1.F4" title="Figure A.4 ‣ Appendix A Additional Figures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a>. During the early years, we see higher interest rate volatility due to the funding liquidity of the DeFi platform. In later samples, interest rates are more stable and approach interest rates in traditional financial markets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Our interest rate data starts from 2020-01-08. Therefore, for coins with perpetual data available before this date (BTC and ETH), we begin the analysis from 2020-01-08. For other coins (BNB, DOGE, ADA), we begin the analysis from the time when they have data available.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The focus of our empirical analysis is the annualized deviation <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>, defined as the interest rate spread that would rationalize an observed futures-spot spread. Under the clamp specification of the funding rate from Binance, we have:</p>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">For example, an estimated <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> of one percentage point would mean that borrowing costs in the cash market faced by arbitrageurs would have to be one percentage point higher than the prevailing interest rate <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> in the cash market for the futures-spot gap to be arbitrage-free.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Rearranging Equation (<a href="#S4.E16" title="In 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>), we obtain the following equation for <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa\left(\frac{F-S}{F}\right)+\text{sgn}\left(\iota-r\right)\gamma-r." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mi>F</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>sgn</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>ι</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa\left(\frac{F-S}{F}\right)+\text{sgn}\left(\iota-r\right)\gamma-r.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">This equation shows that deviations are closely related to the premium index <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{F-S}{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mi>F</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{F-S}{F}</annotation></semantics></math>, adjusted for the clamp parameter <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and the interest rate <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>.
This definition is the same in spirit to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al. (2018)</a></cite>, who measure covered interest parity (CIP) deviations with the wedge that would equate the dollar borrowing rate and the synthetic dollar borrowing rate.<span id="footnote10" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">10</span>
              
              
              
            Alternatively, we may define <math id="footnote10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> as the wedge that satisfies

<span id="S4.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<span><span class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></span>
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=\frac{\kappa}{\kappa+\text{sgn}\left(\iota-(r+\rho)\right)\cdot\gamma-(r+\rho)}S." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>sgn</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>ι</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=\frac{\kappa}{\kappa+\text{sgn}\left(\iota-(r+\rho)\right)\cdot\gamma-(r+\rho)}S.</annotation></semantics></math></span>
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></span></span></span>
</span>Using this definition, after rearranging terms, <math id="footnote10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> simplifies to:

<span id="S4.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<span><span class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></span>
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa(\frac{F-S}{F})+clamp(\iota-\kappa\frac{F-S}{F},-\gamma,\gamma)-r=\Phi-r." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mi>F</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ι</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mi>F</mi></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa(\frac{F-S}{F})+clamp(\iota-\kappa\frac{F-S}{F},-\gamma,\gamma)-r=\Phi-r.</annotation></semantics></math></span>
<span class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></span></span></span>
</span>This result is closely related to the key equation used to determine the fundamental price, <math id="footnote10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi=r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi=r</annotation></semantics></math>. We adopt the first definition for its greater tractability when incorporating trading costs, but both have their merits.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, for each tier of trading cost in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, let <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{S}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{F}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the one-way maker fees in the spot and perpetual futures markets, respectively. Since the arbitrage strategy trades both legs at initiation and again at unwinding, its proportional round-trip exchange-fee cost is <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=2(c_{S}+c_{F})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>F</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=2(c_{S}+c_{F})</annotation></semantics></math>. We map this cost into a threshold value of <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> using the bound from Proposition <a href="#Thmproposition3" title="Proposition 3 (No-arbitrage bounds with trading costs). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, specialized to a proportional trading cost <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
<table id="S4.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E18"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle F-\frac{\kappa}{\kappa+\text{sgn}(\iota-r)\gamma-r}S=cF." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>sgn</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ι</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle F-\frac{\kappa}{\kappa+\text{sgn}(\iota-r)\gamma-r}S=cF.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Equations (<a href="#S4.E16" title="In 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>) and (<a href="#S4.E18" title="In 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>) together imply that the corresponding threshold for <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is:</p>
<table id="S4.E19" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=(\kappa+\text{sgn}(\iota-r)\gamma-r)c\approx\kappa c," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>sgn</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ι</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=(\kappa+\text{sgn}(\iota-r)\gamma-r)c\approx\kappa c,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(19)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.3" class="ltx_p">where the last approximation follows from the empirical fact that <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> is much larger than <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>.<span id="footnote11" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">11</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">11</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">11</span>
              
              
              
            Incorporating <math id="footnote11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="footnote11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> makes a negligible difference for the threshold <math id="footnote11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span></span> Therefore, we calculate the upper and lower trading thresholds in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> as <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa c</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-\kappa c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\kappa c</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Each hour, we calculate <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> defined in Equation (<a href="#S4.E17" title="In 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>) using data on the perpetual futures price, spot price, and the crypto risk-free interest rate. As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, when the perpetual futures price is above the spot, an arbitrageur would short the futures and long the spot, and would finance her position by borrowing in the cash market. On the other hand, when the perpetual futures price is below the spot, an arbitrageur would long the futures, short the spot, and invest the proceeds from shorting in the cash market.</p>
</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> reports summary statistics for <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> in our data. As can be seen, the deviation from the no-arbitrage price is predominantly positive across a substantial portion of the sample, suggesting perpetual futures are more expensive than the no-arbitrage price on average. However, there is considerable variation in these deviations, with the standard deviation exceeding twice the mean deviation for most tokens. The mean absolute deviation is about 60% to 90% per year across different cryptocurrencies.</p>

<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T4.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T4.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The table summarizes statistics for <math id="S4.T4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across various crypto tokens. Panel A presents the summary statistics of <math id="S4.T4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> across the whole sample. Panel B presents the summary statistics for <math id="S4.T4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> before and after 2022-01-01. p-value corresponds to the Newey-West adjusted p-value, testing the null hypothesis that the corresponding mean of <math id="S4.T4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is zero. The sample periods are shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Subsample analysis reveals that the mean deviation and variation in deviation shrink over time. After 2022, the average deviation reduces by almost 80% with volatility shrinking by more than 50% for most tokens. Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> depicts the 7-day moving average of <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> for each of the five examined cryptocurrencies. It reveals considerable comovement in futures-spot spreads across these cryptocurrencies, suggesting a common factor at play that drives the observed divergence. This observation is corroborated by Table <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>, which demonstrates high correlations among futures-spot deviations across the different cryptocurrencies. This trend underscores the interconnectedness of cryptocurrency markets and is consistent with the comovement of traditional currencies documented by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lustig, Roussanov, and Verdelhan (2011)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">One hypothesis for this significant comovement in <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across various cryptocurrencies pertains to time-varying funding constraints encountered by arbitrageurs in the market <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brunnermeier and Pedersen, 2009</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garleanu and Pedersen, 2011</a>)</cite>. Because arbitrageurs often serve as marginal traders in all markets, their funding constraints are potentially reflected in the <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across all major cryptocurrency markets. Our theoretical and empirical analyses underscore the importance of measuring <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>. Doing so not only sheds light on potential market stress but also provides a gauge for the shadow costs associated with the trading and funding constraints arbitrageurs face.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Conversely, from the demand side, shared sentiment across various cryptocurrencies could also contribute to explaining the concurrent movement of <math id="S4.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across different markets. Our theoretical analysis suggests that arbitrageurs will only meet the market demand if the price deviation surpasses the combined trading and funding costs. As a result, the overall market sentiment in the futures market relative to the spot market becomes evident in the price difference between futures and spot prices. If the sentiment across different markets is influenced by a common factor, we would anticipate a significant comovement in the futures-spot spread.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Moreover, arbitrageurs are willing to absorb the idiosyncratic demand first because combining the arbitrage trades across different idiosyncratic deviations would generate a high Sharpe ratio strategy as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kozak et al. (2018)</a></cite>. Therefore, in equilibrium, after arbitrageurs have absorbed the idiosyncratic demand, we anticipate the emergence of a common factor in deviations across different cryptocurrencies, driven by limits to arbitrage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">In Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we delve deeper into explaining the futures-spot spread. Our results demonstrate that the past returns of each cryptocurrency serve as significant explanatory variables for the time-series variation in the spread.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Interestingly, the correlation between deviations and spot market returns is quite modest. Although spot market returns are highly correlated among themselves, in line with the strong market factor results from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2022)</a></cite>, and no-arbitrage price deviations are highly correlated among themselves, it appears that different forces drive these distinct phenomena.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, we find that after the year 2022, futures-spot spreads become much closer and anchored to <math id="S4.SS2.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> compared to earlier samples. This suggests the market is becoming increasingly efficient.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Last but not least, by design, <math id="S4.SS2.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is also highly correlated with the funding rate. The funding rate does not correlate perfectly with <math id="S4.SS2.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> because in real-world implementations: (1) the funding rate is calculated as a weighted average of futures-spot price deviations, with larger weight given to more recent observations; (2) in calculating the funding rate, Binance does not just consider the quote price; they also use an impact margin notional to consider the price impact of the trade.<span id="footnote12" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">12</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">12</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">12</span>
              
              
              
            See <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031</a> for details of the funding rate calculation.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next provide a trading strategy motivated by our random-maturity arbitrage theory. We first consider the zero-cost benchmark. Whenever <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> deviates from zero, we open the convergence position: we short the perpetual and long the spot when <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, and take the opposite position when <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>. We close the position when <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> first returns to zero. Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Effective Bid-Ask Spreads and the Cost of Arbitrage ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a> extends this strategy to account for exchange fees and effective bid-ask spreads.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy for Bitcoin</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F5.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.F5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Deviation from the no-arbitrage price (<math id="S4.F5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>) and trading rules of the random-maturity arbitrage strategy we implement for BTC. Each blue dot in the figure represents the deviation of futures from the no-arbitrage price calculated using Equation <a href="#S4.E17" title="In 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> at hourly frequency. The number is annualized for ease of interpretation. The red line represents the zero benchmark.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> provides an illustration of the trading strategy. When the deviation is above the red line, the strategy opens a long position in the spot and a short position in perpetual. Conversely, when the deviation is below the red line, the strategy is short the spot and long the perpetual.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents the performance of the trading strategy over the years. We find that the trading strategy generates a high Sharpe ratio for all five tokens. The large returns with low volatility and drawdowns suggest that our theory provides useful benchmarks. A deviation from the no-arbitrage price indeed implies a near-arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Performance of Random Maturity Arbitrage Trading Strategy Over Time</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T5.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the Sharpe ratios, annualized returns (%), standard deviations (%), maximum drawdowns (%), and the average open-to-close time (hours) of the unrestricted random-maturity arbitrage trading strategies under zero trading costs for five different cryptocurrencies. The returns reported are excess returns from the random maturity arbitrage strategies.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">An important question is whether zero is in fact the convergence target favored by the data. This is particularly relevant for distinguishing our benchmark from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ackerer et al. (2023)</a></cite>. Under Corollary <a href="#Thmcorollary2" title="Corollary 2 (No-arbitrage price for Binance). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the clamp-adjusted no-arbitrage price corresponds to <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0</annotation></semantics></math>. In contrast, the no-clamp benchmark of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ackerer et al. (2023)</a></cite>, given by Equation (<a href="#S3.E15" title="In 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>), implies</p>
<table id="S4.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\operatorname{sgn}(\iota-r)\gamma." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>sgn</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ι</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\operatorname{sgn}(\iota-r)\gamma.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">Thus, in annualized units, their benchmark corresponds to <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=+54.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>54.75</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=+54.75</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points when <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r&lt;\iota" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>ι</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r&lt;\iota</annotation></semantics></math>, which occurs in 93% of our sample hours, and <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=-54.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>54.75</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=-54.75</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points when <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r&gt;\iota" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>ι</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r&gt;\iota</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Rather than imposing either convergence target, we estimate the target
preferred by the data. For each candidate target <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, we implement the
zero-cost convergence strategy that trades against deviations from <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>
and calculate its annualized Sharpe ratio. Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>
plots the resulting Sharpe-ratio profile. For all five currencies, the
Sharpe ratio is maximized close to zero. Thus, the data-implied convergence point lies close to the clamp-adjusted benchmark derived in Corollary <a href="#Thmcorollary2" title="Corollary 2 (No-arbitrage price for Binance). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v7/figures/fig_r4_target_twolines.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/254;" width="452" height="254" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>The convergence target implied by the data</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F6.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.F6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure plots the annualized Sharpe ratio of the zero-cost convergence strategy that is short the perpetual when <math id="S4.F6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{t}&gt;c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{t}&gt;c</annotation></semantics></math> and long it when <math id="S4.F6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{t}&lt;c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{t}&lt;c</annotation></semantics></math>, as a function of the assumed convergence target <math id="S4.F6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, in annualized percentage points of <math id="S4.F6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>. The solid vertical line is the clamp-consistent benchmark of Corollary <a href="#Thmcorollary2" title="Corollary 2 (No-arbitrage price for Binance). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, at which <math id="S4.F6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is defined to be zero. The dashed line is the no-clamp benchmark <math id="S4.F6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-r}S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-r}S</annotation></semantics></math> of Equation (<a href="#S3.E15" title="In 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>), which sits at <math id="S4.F6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+54.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>54.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+54.75</annotation></semantics></math>. The dotted line at <math id="S4.F6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+43.8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>43.8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+43.8</annotation></semantics></math> is the intermediate variant that replaces <math id="S4.F6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.F6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\iota" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ι</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\iota</annotation></semantics></math>. Sample periods are those of Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> provides a complementary strategy-level comparison. The first alternative ignores the clamp feature and instead uses the no-clamp fundamental price (<a href="#S3.E14" title="In 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>) provided in our earlier draft, or equivalently, in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ackerer et al. (2023)</a></cite>. Consistent with Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, accounting for the clamp substantially improves arbitrage performance: our baseline strategy almost doubles the Sharpe ratio for Bitcoin and
also improves the Sharpe ratio for each of the other four currencies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In the early years of our sample, the infrastructure for shorting cryptocurrencies was underdeveloped. To address this concern, we consider a long-spot-only strategy, in which we set the portfolio weights at <math id="S4.SS3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> if the strategy shorts the spot and longs the futures. We find that even with this restriction, the strategy still generates a high Sharpe ratio in all cryptocurrencies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The last alternative we consider is based on <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christin et al. (2022)</a></cite> who propose a carry strategy in the perpetual futures market where the trader longs the spot, shorts the perpetual, and holds on to the strategy throughout the sample. We present the performance of this strategy in the last column of Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. We find that the long-only strategy significantly outperforms the carry strategy. These results highlight the usefulness of our fundamental price. Given this benchmark, we can identify deviations in real-time and dynamically rebalance the position to take advantage of the deviation rather than making a directional bet as in the Carry strategy.</p>
</div>
