<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>Comparison of Different Arbitrage Trading Strategies</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T6.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">This table compares the performance of 4 trading strategies. Correct is the strategy proposed in this paper. No Clamp is the strategy with the fundamental price given in our earlier draft and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ackerer et al. (2023)</a></cite> which ignores the clamp feature. Long-only is our strategy with a restriction of no short sales in the spot market. Carry is the strategy studied in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christin et al. (2022)</a></cite>. Statistics reported are the annualized Sharpe ratio, return (%), volatility (%), max drawdown (%), alpha (%) relative to the three factors of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2022)</a></cite>, t-stat of the alpha, proportion of time the strategy is active (%), and average open-to-close (OtC) position duration in hours. Sample periods are those of Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">In Appendix <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Appendix C Alternative Arbitrage Strategies ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>, we also present the performance of a data-driven strategy that optimally determines the open and close thresholds using data from the past 6 months. The data-driven strategy has a performance similar to or worse than our theory-motivated strategy, suggesting that our proposed trading strategy is close to being optimal for arbitrage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Comparing the results with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018)</a></cite>, we find that deviations in crypto perpetual futures are considerably larger in magnitude. As a result, gains from the arbitrage strategies we study are also larger. Even though the volatility of the trading strategy also scales up, the Sharpe ratios in the crypto space are still larger than those in the traditional foreign exchange market, as reported in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p11.1" class="ltx_p">When a futures-spot gap opens up, gains from the trading strategy could potentially arise from two main sources: price convergence and funding rate payments. While industry publications usually emphasize the funding rate channel, we note that price convergence can generate quicker gains from arbitrage if dislocations are short-lived.
To examine these two sources empirically, in Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, we provide a decomposition of the trading strategy’s performance into price convergence versus funding rate payments. We find that price convergence plays a dominant role in total trading returns, while funding rate payments have a more minor role, which seems to diminish over time.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Return Decomposition: Price Convergence versus Funding Rate Payment</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T7.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T7.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table decomposes the portfolio return into the part due to price convergence and the part due to funding rate payment. The returns reported are excess returns from the random-maturity arbitrage strategies.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p12.1" class="ltx_p">The success of the trading strategy supports the theory of random-maturity arbitrage. Whenever there is a deviation larger than the gap implied by the theory, betting on convergence tends to generate a positive payoff at some uncertain future time. Therefore, the convergence arbitrage trade generates high Sharpe ratios. We next examine whether these gains survive the transaction costs faced by an arbitrageur in practice.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Effective Bid-Ask Spreads and the Cost of Arbitrage</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next examine the execution costs of the random-maturity arbitrage strategy. This requires measuring bid-ask spreads over the full sample. We therefore construct daily effective bid-ask spreads from Binance transaction records and document their behavior over time. We then incorporate these spreads, together with exchange fees, into the arbitrage strategy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each of the five currencies, we obtain the complete daily record of
aggregated trades in Binance’s spot market and in its USD-margined perpetual
futures market.<span id="footnote13" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">13</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">13</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">13</span>
              
              
              
            The archives are available at
<a href="https://data.binance.vision/data/spot/daily/aggTrades/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://data.binance.vision/data/spot/daily/aggTrades/</a> and
<a href="https://data.binance.vision/data/futures/um/daily/aggTrades/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://data.binance.vision/data/futures/um/daily/aggTrades/</a>. An
aggregated trade combines the fills of a single taker order at a single price.</span></span></span>
Each record reports the trade price <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and whether the taker, the side that
initiated the trade, was the buyer or the seller. We code the trade direction as
<math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}=+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}=+1</annotation></semantics></math> for a taker buy and <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}=-1</annotation></semantics></math> for a taker sell.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To estimate the effective spread, let <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the log efficient price at
the time of trade <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> and let <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> denote the proportional effective
bid-ask spread. The transaction price satisfies</p>
<table id="S4.E20" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E20.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log p_{t}=m_{t}+\frac{s}{2}q_{t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log p_{t}=m_{t}+\frac{s}{2}q_{t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(20)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.2" class="ltx_p">If <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> follows a random walk with innovations <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> that are
uncorrelated with trade direction, taking first differences gives</p>
<table id="S4.E21" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E21.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\log p_{t}=\frac{s}{2}\Delta q_{t}+\epsilon_{t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\log p_{t}=\frac{s}{2}\Delta q_{t}+\epsilon_{t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(21)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.3" class="ltx_p">This is the trade-indicator representation underlying <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Roll (1984)</a></cite>. In the original Roll estimator, trade direction is unobserved, so the effective spread is inferred from the negative serial covariance of transaction price changes. Binance, by contrast, reports whether the taker is the buyer or the
seller for every trade. We can therefore use the observed trade direction to
estimate Equation (<a href="#S4.E21" title="In 4.4 Effective Bid-Ask Spreads and the Cost of Arbitrage ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>) directly by ordinary least squares,
separately for each currency, market, and day:</p>
<table id="S4.E22" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{s}=2\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}\left(\Delta\log p_{t},\Delta q_{t}\right)}{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\left(\Delta q_{t}\right)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Cov</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Var</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{s}=2\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}\left(\Delta\log p_{t},\Delta q_{t}\right)}{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\left(\Delta q_{t}\right)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(22)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.4" class="ltx_p">A taker order executes at or beyond the best quote, and quotes lie on the
exchange’s price grid, so the spread paid by a trade is at least one tick. We
therefore floor each daily estimate at one tick, measured as the most common
nonzero price change during the day and expressed in basis points of the average
price. The floor rarely binds for BTC, on at most 5% of days in either market,
or for the ETH perpetual.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The Kaiko order-book sample described in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a> also provides an external validation of our trade-based spread estimates. In these snapshots, the
quoted spread of the Bitcoin perpetual equals one tick 99% of the time and
averages approximately 0.05 basis points. Over the same period, our effective
spread estimate averages approximately 0.1 basis points. The two measures are
therefore of the same order of magnitude. The effective spread is somewhat
larger, as expected, because taker orders can execute at several price levels
beyond the best quote and because the estimator can also absorb part of the
price impact of trades.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<div id="S4.F7.2" class="ltx_logical-block ltx_figure_panel">
          
<div id="S4.F7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2212.06888v7/fig_r4_bidask.svg" id="S4.F7.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/161;" width="476" height="161"></object>
</div>
        
</div></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Effective Bid-Ask Spreads of Spot and Perpetual Futures</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F7.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.F7.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure plots the daily effective bid-ask spread on Binance of the spot
(left panel) and perpetual futures (right panel) markets, estimated from
Equation (<a href="#S4.E22" title="In 4.4 Effective Bid-Ask Spreads and the Cost of Arbitrage ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>) and floored at one tick, in basis points.
Each series is smoothed with a seven-day moving median and plotted on a
logarithmic scale. Flat stretches are days on which the tick floor binds.
Dotted vertical lines mark the COVID crash of March 12, 2020, the crash of
May 19, 2021, the collapse of Terra in May 2022, and the collapse of FTX in
November 2022. Each series starts in January 2020 or on the first day with
trade records for the contract and ends on March 11, 2024.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.4 Effective Bid-Ask Spreads and the Cost of Arbitrage ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> reveals three patterns. First, perpetual
futures are highly liquid. Over the full sample, the median daily effective
spread of the perpetual is 0.11 basis points for BTC, 0.18 for ETH, 0.44 for
BNB, 1.35 for DOGE, and 2.12 for ADA. The perpetual spread is below that of the
corresponding spot market for BNB, DOGE, and ADA and is comparable to it for
BTC and ETH. Second, effective spreads generally narrow over time. Comparing
the periods before and after 2022, the mean effective spread of the perpetual
declines by between 48% and 73% for BTC, ETH, BNB, and DOGE. Third, spreads
increase sharply during periods of market stress. On March 12, 2020, for
example, the effective spread of the Bitcoin perpetual reached 5.95 basis
points, more than ten times its median over the preceding weeks, and the
spreads of all other contracts trading at the time more than doubled.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We now incorporate these costs into the random-maturity arbitrage strategy.
In the presence of trading costs, as motivated by our theory, we use the
threshold trading rules implied by Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Different fee tiers have
the same close-position threshold, equal to zero, while the open-position
threshold becomes wider as trading costs increase. We visualize these trading
rules in Figure <a href="#A1.F5" title="Figure A.5 ‣ Appendix A Additional Figures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.5</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Additional Figures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond the baseline case with only exchange fees, we also report the performance of the strategy with both exchange fees and bid-ask spread. Let <math id="S4.SS4.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{S}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{F}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the one-way spot and perpetual exchange fees in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, and let <math id="S4.SS4.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{S}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>S</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{S}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{F}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>F</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{F}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the corresponding daily effective spreads.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The proportional round-trip trading cost <math id="S4.SS4.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> in Equation (<a href="#S4.E19" title="In 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>) therefore becomes</p>
<table id="S4.E23" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E23.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}=2\left(c_{S}+\frac{s^{S}_{t}}{2}\right)+2\left(c_{F}+\frac{s^{F}_{t}}{2}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>S</mi></msubsup><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>F</mi></msubsup><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}=2\left(c_{S}+\frac{s^{S}_{t}}{2}\right)+2\left(c_{F}+\frac{s^{F}_{t}}{2}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(23)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Since the strategy under trading costs is a threshold trading rule, to
annualize Sharpe ratios, we follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lucca and Moench (2015)</a></cite>, who consider a trading
strategy that is active only on FOMC announcement dates. We first calculate the
mean (<math id="S4.SS4.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math>) and standard deviation (<math id="S4.SS4.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>) of the strategy return during
the periods in which the strategy is active. We then scale <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu/\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu/\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> by the
number of active periods in a year:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="SR=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt{N_{a}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>μ</mi><mi>σ</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">SR=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt{N_{a}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p9.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> is the average number of hours the strategy is active in a year.
We use the same convention to annualize returns and standard deviations:
<math id="S4.SS4.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\mathrm{ann}}=\mu N_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>ann</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\mathrm{ann}}=\mu N_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S4.SS4.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\mathrm{ann}}=\sigma\sqrt{N_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>ann</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\mathrm{ann}}=\sigma\sqrt{N_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>

</tbody>
</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span>Random-Maturity Arbitrage with Exchange Fees and Effective Spreads</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T8.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.T8.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Performance under different trading cost tiers, with and without bid-ask spread costs. The fees for spot (futures) are 0 (0) bps, 2.25 (0.18) bps, 4.5 (0.72) bps, and 6.75 (1.44) bps for the zero, low, medium, and high trading cost levels. For each fee tier, the spread-adjusted strategy additionally pays half the daily effective spread on each transaction in each leg. Spreads are estimated over the execution day using Equation (<a href="#S4.E22" title="In 4.4 Effective Bid-Ask Spreads and the Cost of Arbitrage ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>). Statistics reported are the annualized Sharpe ratio, return (%), volatility (%), max drawdown (%), alpha (%) relative to the three factors of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2022)</a></cite>, <math id="S4.T8.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>-stat of the alpha, proportion of time the strategy is active (%), and average open-to-close (OtC) position duration in hours. Sample periods are those of Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 4.4 Effective Bid-Ask Spreads and the Cost of Arbitrage ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> presents the strategy’s performance under different
exchange fee tiers. As fees increase, the random-maturity arbitrage strategy
trades less frequently and the average open-to-close duration increases.
Nevertheless, even at the high fee tier, the strategy generates large Sharpe
ratios across all five currencies. It also delivers highly significant alphas
relative to the 3-factor model of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2022)</a></cite> and the 5-factor model
of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong et al. (2022a)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p11.1" class="ltx_p">The effective spread has relatively little effect on BTC and ETH. At the high
fee tier, adding the spread reduces the Sharpe ratio from 3.35 to 3.27 for BTC
and from 4.56 to 4.45 for ETH. The effect is larger for BNB, DOGE, and ADA. As exchange fees increase, the spread represents a smaller share of total execution costs and the difference between the fee-only and fee-plus-spread strategies generally narrows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Most importantly, incorporating effective spreads does not overturn the
economic conclusion from the arbitrage strategy. At the high fee tier, Sharpe
ratios net of both exchange fees and effective spreads range from 3.27 for BTC
to 6.63 for BNB. The corresponding alphas remain statistically significant for
all five currencies, with <math id="S4.SS4.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>-statistics of at least 3.14. Thus, although
effective bid-ask spreads are an economically important component of trading
costs, particularly for less liquid cryptocurrencies, they do not account
for the large deviations from the no-arbitrage benchmark.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Execution costs are only one potential impediment to arbitrage. Even a trade that is profitable upon convergence can generate interim losses if the deviation widens before the position is closed. Because perpetual futures positions are margined, sufficiently large interim losses could force an arbitrageur to liquidate the position before convergence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p14.1" class="ltx_p">The maximum drawdowns reported in Table <a href="#S4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 4.4 Effective Bid-Ask Spreads and the Cost of Arbitrage ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> provide a simple gauge of this risk. Across the specifications in the table, maximum drawdowns do not exceed 3.90% for BTC, 2.67% for ETH, and 2.26% for BNB. They are larger for DOGE and ADA, reaching 13.90% and 5.69%, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p15.1" class="ltx_p">Execution costs are only one potential impediment to arbitrage. Even a trade
that is profitable upon convergence can generate interim losses if the
deviation widens before it closes. We therefore next examine whether
liquidation risk can prevent arbitrageurs from exploiting these deviations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p16.1" class="ltx_p">The maximum drawdowns reported in Table <a href="#S4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 4.4 Effective Bid-Ask Spreads and the Cost of Arbitrage ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> provide a simple gauge of this risk. Across the specifications in the table, maximum drawdowns do not exceed 3.90% for BTC, 2.67% for ETH, and 2.26% for BNB. They are larger for DOGE and ADA, reaching 13.90% and 5.69%, respectively. Thus, interim losses are relatively modest for the more liquid cryptocurrencies, although liquidation risk can be more relevant for less liquid assets. Beyond drawdowns, liquidations also depend on leverage, maintenance-margin requirements, available collateral, and the applicable margining regime. We examine the broader role of margin constraints and arbitrage capital in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Explaining Futures-spot Deviations</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> documents large and persistent futures-spot deviations that comove strongly across cryptocurrencies. What generates these deviations? We explore the hypothesis that they reflect the interaction between end-user demand for leveraged perpetual exposure and the limited capacity of arbitrageurs to intermediate that demand.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We proceed in four steps. Section <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Exploratory Evidence ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a> begins with a set of exploratory evidence on deviations <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> in reduced-form panel regressions. Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Economic Mechanism and Predictions ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a> then summarizes the economic mechanism and two empirical predictions of a simple model, which we develop formally in Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G A Model of Deviations in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>. Sections <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Prediction 1: Arbitrage Constraints and Equilibrium Deviations ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> and <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Prediction 2: State Dependent Price Impact ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a> test these predictions using Binance’s introduction of portfolio margining and the state dependence of the price impact of perpetual order flow and find support for the model in the data.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Exploratory Evidence</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Two forces could plausibly generate the common variation in <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>. The first is variation in arbitrageurs’ ability to intermediate between futures and spot markets. Since the same intermediaries operate across cryptocurrencies, common variation in their funding or balance-sheet conditions could generate common variation in deviations. The second force is variation in end-user demand for perpetual exposure relative to spot. Perpetuals allow for high leverage and therefore provide a natural venue for investors with strong directional beliefs. If such beliefs comove across cryptocurrencies, they can generate common demand pressure in perpetual markets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We begin with a reduced-form regression designed to let the data speak to both channels. We proxy relative demand for perpetual exposure using trailing spot returns. If investors extrapolate recent returns, positive past performance should increase demand for perpetual exposure relative to spot. We proxy time-varying risk-based constraints on arbitrageurs using trailing spot-return volatility, following the Value-at-Risk logic of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Adrian and Shin (2010)</a></cite>: higher volatility tightens risk constraints and should reduce intermediaries’ willingness to absorb order flow.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> suggests that deviations decline substantially over the sample. Models of convergence trading such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kondor (2009)</a></cite> predict that competition among arbitrageurs may reduce the gap gradually. Therefore, we add a time trend variable to the regression to test if the market becomes more efficient over time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In sum, we estimate the following regression models:</p>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 9: </span>Regression of the no-arbitrage deviations against explanatory variables</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S5.T9.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S5.T9.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We present regression results of <math id="S5.T9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.T9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> on a time trend (Time) measured in units of years, past 120 days’ annualized returns (Ret), and volatility (Vol) in the spot market. We add a currency fixed effect to the regression and consider three specifications: (1) regressing <math id="S5.T9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>/<math id="S5.T9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> on the time trend, (2) regressing <math id="S5.T9.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>/<math id="S5.T9.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> on past returns, and (3) regressing <math id="S5.T9.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>/<math id="S5.T9.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> on past returns and volatility. The observations are at a daily frequency. The sample period spans from January 8, 2020 to March 11, 2024, totaling 1,495 days. The table also reports the <math id="S5.T9.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> values for each regression model. We report Newey-West t-statistics in parentheses with a lag of 120 days. <math id="S5.T9.m14" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="*\text{ }p&lt;.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mtext> </mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">*\text{ }p&lt;.1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.T9.m15" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="**\text{ }p&lt;.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mtext> </mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">**\text{ }p&lt;.05</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.T9.m16" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="***\text{ }p&lt;.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mtext> </mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">***\text{ }p&lt;.01</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ 5.1 Exploratory Evidence ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> presents the regression results. Three facts stand out. First, deviations decline substantially over the sample. The coefficient on the time trend is negative and statistically significant at the one percent level in all six specifications. In the trend-only regression for <math id="S5.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math>, the estimate of (-0.22) implies an average decline in the annualized absolute deviation of approximately 22 percentage points per year.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Second, deviations rise with past returns. The coefficients on trailing returns are positive and significant at the one percent level for both <math id="S5.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math>. This pattern is consistent with extrapolative demand: following high spot returns, investors increase their demand for leveraged perpetual exposure, and the portion of that demand not absorbed by arbitrageurs appears in the futures-spot deviation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">This finding is related to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu and Tsyvinski (2021)</a></cite>, who document strong time-series momentum in cryptocurrency returns. Our evidence raises the possibility that some of this momentum is associated with leverage demand and price pressure originating in perpetual futures markets. We leave this as an open question for future research.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Third, the standard risk-based proxy for arbitrage constraints enters with the opposite sign. A simple Value-at-Risk mechanism predicts: higher volatility should tighten intermediary constraints and widen deviations. Therefore, the regressions provide no evidence that a time-varying, risk-based tightening of arbitrage constraints is the primary driver of the common variation in <math id="S5.SS1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Economic Mechanism and Predictions</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use a simple model to organize the evidence and motivate the empirical tests that follow. The model is developed formally in Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G A Model of Deviations in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The model has two types of market participants. End users demand perpetual futures because they provide leveraged exposure to the underlying cryptocurrency. Arbitrageurs take the other side of this demand and hedge their positions in the spot market. Their willingness to intermediate, however, is limited by trading costs, risk, and the amount of capital required to maintain the arbitrage position.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The key mechanism is that arbitrageurs absorb end-user demand as long as they have sufficient balance-sheet capacity. When capacity is abundant, an increase in demand can largely be accommodated by larger arbitrage positions, with relatively little effect on the futures-spot deviation. When arbitrageurs become capital constrained, they can no longer expand their positions sufficiently, and the market instead clears through larger price deviations. This mechanism delivers two predictions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prediction 1 (arbitrage constraints).</span> <em id="S5.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Relaxing arbitrageurs’ capital constraints should reduce futures-spot deviations.</em> Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Prediction 1: Arbitrage Constraints and Equilibrium Deviations ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> tests this prediction using Binance’s introduction of portfolio margining, which allowed arbitrageurs to use their capital more efficiently by netting spot and futures positions within the same margin account.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prediction 2 (state-dependent price impact).</span> <em id="S5.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">End-user demand should have a larger price impact when arbitrageurs are more constrained.</em> When arbitrageurs have spare capacity, they can absorb additional order flow with little movement in prices. When their capacity is limited, the same order flow should produce a larger change in the futures-spot deviation. Section <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Prediction 2: State Dependent Price Impact ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a> tests this prediction by examining whether perpetual-futures order flow has a larger price impact when the initial deviation is large.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Both tests provide support for these predictions and therefore for the suggested mechanism.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Prediction 1: Arbitrage Constraints and Equilibrium Deviations</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prediction 1 says that deviations should narrow when arbitrageurs can support a larger book with the same capital. Binance’s introduction of portfolio margining on April 20, 2022 provides a direct test.<span id="footnote14" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">14</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">14</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">14</span>
              
              
              
            Details of the event are provided in Binance’s announcement: <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/announcement/detail/c013c3ceaa604a3eaa362647b06441a1" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/announcement/detail/c013c3ceaa604a3eaa362647b06441a1</a>.</span></span></span> Before the change, arbitrageurs maintain separate margin accounts for spot and futures positions, so a gain on one leg could not offset a loss on the other, and each leg had to be capitalized against early liquidation on its own. Portfolio margining allowed the two legs to be netted inside a unified account. According to the model, this decline in margin requirements implies a rise in arbitrage capacity, therefore a compression of the deviation.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Prediction 2: State Dependent Price Impact</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prediction 2 says that the price impact of order flow depends on the state of arbitrage capacity. When arbitrage capital is slack, arbitrageurs absorb end-user demand with little movement in the futures-spot deviation. Once arbitrage capacity becomes constrained, however, additional order flow must be accommodated through a larger price response. We therefore test Prediction 2 by allowing the price impact of perpetual order flow to vary with the absolute deviation at the beginning of the interval.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We aggregate the hourly panel to eight-hour funding intervals and estimate the following specification on the pooled panel of five currencies:</p>

<p id="S5.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{i,t}=(F_{i,t}-S_{i,t})/F_{i,t}" display="inline" perpetual taker order imbalance over the same interval, measured in percentage points. The specification includes currency fixed effects, <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, and indicators <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{k,i,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{k,i,t}</annotation></semantics></math> for bins of the initial absolute premium, <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|P_{i,t}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|P_{i,t}|</annotation></semantics></math>. The coefficients <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> therefore measure the price impact of order flow conditional on the initial size of the futures-spot deviation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ 5.4 Prediction 2: State Dependent Price Impact ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> first divides intervals within each currency into terciles of <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|P_{i,t}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|P_{i,t}|</annotation></semantics></math>. In the low-deviation tercile, where mean <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|P|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|P|</annotation></semantics></math> is 2.47 basis points, a one-percentage-point increase in taker order imbalance moves the premium index by 0.031 basis points. In the high-deviation tercile, where mean <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|P|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|P|</annotation></semantics></math> is 12.05 basis points, the same order flow moves the premium by 0.094 basis points, roughly three times as much. The high-minus-low difference is 0.062 basis points and is statistically significant.</p>
</div>

<p id="S5.T11.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S5.T11.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the price impact of perpetual taker order imbalance across intervals with different initial futures-spot deviations. The panel is aggregated to eight-hour funding intervals. Within each cryptocurrency, intervals are divided into terciles based on the absolute premium index at the beginning of the interval. Price Impact is the change in the premium index, in basis points, associated with a one-percentage-point increase in perpetual taker order imbalance. The final column reports the difference between the high- and low-deviation terciles. Driscoll-Kraay standard errors with a Bartlett kernel and six lags are reported in parentheses. <math id="S5.T11.m17" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{}^{*},p&lt;.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}^{*},p&lt;.1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.T11.m18" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{}^{**},p&lt;.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∗</mo><mo lspace="0em">⁣</mo><mo>∗</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}^{**},p&lt;.05</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.T11.m19" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{}^{***},p&lt;.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em">∗</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}^{***},p&lt;.01</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The results match the state dependence implied by Prediction 2. Over most of the deviation distribution, additional perpetual order flow produces little change in the futures-spot premium, consistent with arbitrage capital elastically absorbing end-user demand. Price impact rises sharply only in the upper tail, where large deviations indicate that arbitrage capacity is more likely to bind.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures play an important role in today’s crypto markets and could potentially be adopted in non-crypto markets in the future. Understanding the fundamental mechanism of this financial derivative is a crucial first step for understanding speculation and hedging dynamics in this fast-evolving area. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the arbitrage and funding rate payment mechanisms that underpin perpetual futures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In an ideal, frictionless world, we show that arbitrageurs would trade perpetual futures in such a way that a constant proportional relationship would hold between the futures price and the spot price. In the presence of trading costs, the deviation of the futures price from the spot would lie within a bound.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by our theory, we empirically examine the comovement of the futures-spot spread across different cryptocurrencies and implement a theory-motivated arbitrage strategy. We find that this simple strategy yields substantial Sharpe ratios across various trading cost scenarios. The evidence supports our theoretical argument that perpetual futures-spot spreads exceeding trading costs represent a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we develop a simple model in which end users demand leveraged perpetual exposure while arbitrageurs intermediate between futures and spot subject to limited balance-sheet capacity. The model predicts that looser arbitrage constraints compress deviations and that end-user demand has greater price impact when arbitrage capacity is constrained. Consistent with these predictions, deviations fall following Binance’s introduction of portfolio margining, and perpetual order flow has greater price impact when initial deviations are large. We also find that past returns positively predict deviations, consistent with extrapolative demand for leveraged perpetual exposure. Together, these findings highlight the interaction between end-user demand and limited arbitrage capacity as an important force shaping perpetual futures prices.</p>
</div>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Funding Rate Calculation on Binance</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we describe the funding rate mechanism used by Binance in greater detail and discuss the economic role of its clamped funding rule. Our description follows the methodology provided by Binance.<span id="footnote15" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">15</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">15</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">15</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031</a></span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">There are five general steps in obtaining the funding rate. The first step is to find the Impact Bid/Ask Price Series in a given funding period by analyzing the order book and determining the average fill price to execute a certain notional value (Impact Margin Notional) on the bid and ask sides.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The impact margin notional is defined as the notional available to trade with a margin of 200 USD. So it can be calculated using the following equation:</p>
<table id="A2.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{IMN}=200/\text{Initial margin rate at maximum leverage level}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>IMN</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>/</mo><mtext>Initial margin rate at maximum leverage level</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{IMN}=200/\text{Initial margin rate at maximum leverage level}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Given the definition of impact margin notional, the impact bid/ask price is defined as the average trade price after a market sell/buy order with the total quoted notional quantity given by the IMN.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Given impact bid and ask prices (denoted as IBP and IAP, respectively), the second step is to calculate the premium index (denoted as P) series every <math id="A2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> seconds using the following equation:</p>
<table id="A2.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=[\text{Max}(0,\text{IBP}-\text{Price Index})-\text{Max}(0,\text{Price Index}-\text{IAP})]/\text{Price Index}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>Max</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext>IBP</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>Price Index</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mtext>Max</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext>Price Index</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>IAP</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mtext>Price Index</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=[\text{Max}(0,\text{IBP}-\text{Price Index})-\text{Max}(0,\text{Price Index}-\text{IAP})]/\text{Price Index},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where ‘Price Index’ is the weighted average spot price of the underlying asset listed on major spot exchanges.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The rationale behind this formula is to capture the relative difference between the perpetual contract’s price and the underlying asset’s price, taking into account the actual market liquidity and depth represented by the IBP and IAP.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The third step is to calculate the time-weighted average premium index over the funding period (8 hours for Binance) using the premium index series:</p>
<table id="A2.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{P}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}P_{t}/\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">/</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{P}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}P_{t}/\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p7.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the <math id="A2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>-th 5-second in the 8-hour funding period, <math id="A2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=t</annotation></semantics></math> is the weight for each observation, and <math id="A2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is the total number of 5-second intervals within the 8-hour period. For Binance, <math id="A2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=12\times 6\times 8=5760" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5760</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=12\times 6\times 8=5760</annotation></semantics></math>. With this weighting scheme, the observations closer to the funding rate payment receive larger weights. The weights increase linearly in time over the 8-hour interval.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Given the average premium index, the fourth step is to calculate the funding rate using the equation below:</p>
<table id="A2.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="fr=\bar{P}+\text{clamp}(\iota-\bar{P},-0.05\%,0.05\%)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>clamp</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ι</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>0.05</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>0.05</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">fr=\bar{P}+\text{clamp}(\iota-\bar{P},-0.05\%,0.05\%),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p8.2" class="ltx_p">where fr is the funding rate, <math id="A2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\iota" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ι</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\iota</annotation></semantics></math> is the interest component set by Binance, and</p>
<table id="A2.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{clamp}(x,\text{min},\text{max})=\begin{cases}min,&amp;\text{if }x&lt;\text{min}\\
x,&amp;\text{if }\text{min}\leq x\leq\text{max}\\
max,&amp;\text{if }x&gt;\text{max}\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>clamp</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>min</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>max</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mtext>min</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mtext>min</mtext></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mtext>max</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mtext>max</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{clamp}(x,\text{min},\text{max})=\begin{cases}min,&amp;\text{if }x&lt;\text{min}\\
x,&amp;\text{if }\text{min}\leq x\leq\text{max}\\
max,&amp;\text{if }x&gt;\text{max}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p8.3" class="ltx_p">Empirically, for Binance futures, the interest rate <math id="A2.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is fixed at 0.01% per 8 hours for most perpetual futures. Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> plots the funding rate as a function of the premium index. As can be seen, when the premium index is close to the clamp region, the funding rate is fixed at the interest component.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">This feature has several economic implications. First, it makes funding payments more stable and predictable when the perpetual futures price is close to the underlying spot price. Small fluctuations in the premium do not mechanically translate into changes in the funding payment. In this sense, the clamp introduces a “no-adjustment region” around the normal funding rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Second, the clamp preserves the convergence mechanism when deviations become economically meaningful. It is important that the clamp is not an outer cap on the funding rate. Once the premium index moves outside the no-adjustment region, the funding rate again increases one-for-one with the premium index. Large positive premiums therefore generate larger payments from long to short positions, while sufficiently large discounts generate payments in the opposite direction. The funding mechanism consequently becomes stronger precisely when the futures price moves sufficiently far from the spot benchmark.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Third, the design reduces the sensitivity of funding payments to small or transitory distortions in the measured premium. Under a purely linear rule, any change in the premium index immediately changes the funding transfer between long and short positions. Under the clamped rule, by contrast, the local response of the funding rate to the premium index is zero inside the clamp region. A trader attempting to alter the funding payment must therefore move the average premium sufficiently far to cross the boundary of the no-adjustment region before the funding payment begins to change.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p12.1" class="ltx_p">This consideration is reinforced by the way the premium index itself is constructed. The index is based on impact prices rather than the best quoted prices, so changing it requires moving prices over some depth of the order book. It is also averaged over the funding period, so a sufficiently large or persistent distortion is required to have a material effect on the settlement premium. Together with the clamp, these features make funding payments less sensitive to small or short-lived price distortions. We view this as an additional economic rationale for the clamped design, although we do not attempt to quantify its importance for manipulation empirically.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T1" title="Table B.1 ‣ Appendix B Funding Rate Calculation on Binance ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a> compares the realized Binance funding rate <math id="A2.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(P)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(P)</annotation></semantics></math> with the counterfactual linear funding rate <math id="A2.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa P</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A2.p13.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=(F-S)/F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=(F-S)/F</annotation></semantics></math> is the premium index, evaluated on the same hours. It reports how often the clamp binds, and the mean and standard deviation of the funding payment under each rule.</p>
</div>
