<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table B.1: </span>The clamp versus a linear funding rate</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="A2.T1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="A2.T1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table compares the realized Binance funding rate <math id="A2.T1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(P)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(P)</annotation></semantics></math> with the counterfactual linear rule <math id="A2.T1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa P</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A2.T1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=(F-S)/F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=(F-S)/F</annotation></semantics></math> is the premium index. “Hours (%)” is the share of hours in which the premium index lies inside the clamp region, <math id="A2.T1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\kappa P-\iota|\leq\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>ι</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\kappa P-\iota|\leq\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>, where the funding payment is fixed at <math id="A2.T1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\iota" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ι</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\iota</annotation></semantics></math> and does not respond to the basis. “Settlements at <math id="A2.T1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\iota" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ι</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\iota</annotation></semantics></math> (%)” is the share of realized eight-hour funding settlements paid at exactly the interest component. BNBUSDT is the one contract in our sample with <math id="A2.T1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\iota=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ι</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\iota=0</annotation></semantics></math>. Standard deviations and means are computed over settlement hours and annualized by a factor of <math id="A2.T1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\times 365" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>365</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times 365</annotation></semantics></math>. Sample periods are those of Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="A2.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p14.1" class="ltx_p">The table shows that the no-adjustment region is economically relevant rather than a minor institutional detail. Depending on the asset, the clamp region accounts for approximately 36–45% of observations, and roughly 42–50% of realized funding settlements occur exactly at the interest component. Moreover, funding payments under the clamped rule are substantially less volatile than under the counterfactual linear rule. These results are consistent with the interpretation that the clamp stabilizes funding payments during normal market conditions while preserving stronger funding incentives when the futures-spot deviation becomes sufficiently large.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p15.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, Binance imposes an additional outer cap and floor on the funding rate based on the maximum leverage of the contract. For contracts with maximum leverage of 30x or above, the cap and floor depend on the Maintenance Margin Ratio. For contracts with maximum leverage of 25x or below, they are fixed at <math id="A2.p15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 3\%</annotation></semantics></math>. This final restriction serves a different purpose from the clamp. Whereas the clamp makes the funding rate locally insensitive to small price deviations, the outer cap limits the size of funding transfers during extreme market conditions. Extremely large funding payments can generate substantial losses for highly leveraged positions and potentially trigger liquidations. The outer cap therefore limits this tail risk without eliminating the funding mechanism’s response to economically meaningful price deviations.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Alternative Arbitrage Strategies</h2>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the main text of our paper, we demonstrate the profitability of a simple theory-motivated trading strategy. The trading threshold can also be potentially further improved using a data-driven approach. In this part, we implement a data-driven two-threshold arbitrage trading strategy in the perpetual futures market to verify that our proposed theory-motivated strategy is optimal.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The data-driven strategy can be characterized by a tuple of two thresholds: <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,l)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the upper bar and <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the lower bar, <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u&gt;l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u&gt;l</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&gt;u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&gt;u</annotation></semantics></math>, we long the spot and short the futures. When <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-l&lt;\rho&lt;l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-l&lt;\rho&lt;l</annotation></semantics></math>, we close the position. When <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&lt;-u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&lt;-u</annotation></semantics></math>, we long the futures and short the spot. Figure <a href="#A3.F1" title="Figure C.1 ‣ C.1 Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Appendix C Alternative Arbitrage Strategies ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a> presents an illustration of the strategy for Bitcoin with the trading thresholds estimated using real-time data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v7/figure_trading_data_driven_agg_BTC.png" id="A3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/243;" width="476" height="243" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure C.1: </span>Data-driven Random Maturity Arbitrage Strategy for Bitcoin</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="A3.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="A3.F1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Deviation from the no-arbitrage price (<math id="A3.F1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>) and trading rules of the data-driven random-maturity arbitrage strategy we implement for BTC. Each blue dot in the figure represents the deviation of futures from the no-arbitrage price calculated using Equation <a href="#S4.E17" title="In 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> at hourly frequency. The number is annualized for ease of interpretation. The orange line is the open-position threshold, and the red line is the close-position threshold.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="A3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To determine the optimal <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,l)</annotation></semantics></math>, at the beginning of each month, we calculate the returns of the two-threshold trading strategy based on the past six months’ data on a grid of parameters. From Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we find that the theory-implied bounds for price deviation across all trading-cost specifications lie within <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-200\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+200\%</annotation></semantics></math>. So we choose the grid as increasing from <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="250\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>250</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">250\%</annotation></semantics></math> with an incremental step of <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="A3.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u\geq l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u\geq l</annotation></semantics></math>). In total, there are <math id="A3.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="351" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>351</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">351</annotation></semantics></math> model specifications. We choose the model that delivers the highest Sharpe Ratio in the validation sample of the past six months.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We present the visualization of all trading strategies under zero to high trading costs in Appendix Figure <a href="#A3.F2" title="Figure C.2 ‣ C.1 Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Appendix C Alternative Arbitrage Strategies ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a> to Figure <a href="#A3.F5" title="Figure C.5 ‣ C.1 Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Appendix C Alternative Arbitrage Strategies ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.5</span></a>. Under no trading costs, the strategy chooses a low open-position threshold, and the open- and close-position thresholds coincide with each other. Since there is no trading cost, the strategy no longer needs to wait for price convergence to avoid high turnover. On the contrary, with high trading costs, the strategy chooses a larger open-position threshold and a smaller close-position threshold. This reflects the automatic adjustment by the algorithm for trading costs and turnover.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T1" title="Table C.1 ‣ C.1 Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Appendix C Alternative Arbitrage Strategies ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a> presents the performance statistics for this strategy under no trading costs over time. Table <a href="#A3.T2" title="Table C.2 ‣ C.1 Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Appendix C Alternative Arbitrage Strategies ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a> further presents the overall performance of the data-driven strategy across different trading costs. We find that the arbitrage trading strategy has a high Sharpe ratio, similar to and comparable to our theory-motivated ones. This suggests our theory-motivated strategy is close to optimal.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to the theory-motivated case, we decompose the performance of the trading strategy into: (1) the price convergence and (2) the funding rate payment. The results are presented in Table <a href="#A3.T3" title="Table C.3 ‣ C.1 Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Appendix C Alternative Arbitrage Strategies ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a>. Similar to the theory-motivated strategy, we find that the return from price convergence accounts for a larger proportion of the total profit.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, our analysis of the data-driven trading strategy validates the optimality of our theory-driven approach, underscoring the value of our theoretical benchmark. Notably, introducing additional flexible adjustments does not significantly improve the performance of the arbitrage strategy.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Statistical Arbitrage with Cointegration</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The random-maturity arbitrage (RMA) of Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and the statistical notion of cointegration with error correction describe the same object from two angles. We next consider a more parametric data-driven strategy inspired by statistical arbitrage with cointegration.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Proposition <a href="#Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price: General Case). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> gives the frictionless price <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}=\lambda S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}=\lambda S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and Proposition <a href="#Thmproposition3" title="Proposition 3 (No-arbitrage bounds with trading costs). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> confines the ratio to a bound around <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> once there are trading costs. Taking logs, the basis <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{t}\equiv\log F_{t}-\log S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{t}\equiv\log F_{t}-\log S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is bounded and mean-reverting around <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>, with the funding payment <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math> supplying the restoring force.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the language of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Engle and Granger (1987)</a></cite>, if <math id="A3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log F_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log F_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are each <math id="A3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(1)</annotation></semantics></math>, then they are cointegrated with cointegrating vector <math id="A3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1,-1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1,-1)</annotation></semantics></math>, and the funding rate plays the role of the error-correction term.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T4" title="Table C.4 ‣ C.2 Statistical Arbitrage with Cointegration ‣ Appendix C Alternative Arbitrage Strategies ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.4</span></a> confirms this empirically. For every coin, the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test fails to reject a unit root in the log price levels, while it rejects a unit root in the basis: the two series are individually <math id="A3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(1)</annotation></semantics></math> but cointegrated.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T4" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table C.4: </span>Cointegration of Perpetual Futures and Spot Prices</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="A3.T4.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="A3.T4.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Tests for cointegration of <math id="A3.T4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\log F_{t},\log S_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\log F_{t},\log S_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> over the full sample. The first three columns report ADF <span id="A3.T4.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">p</span>-values (null: unit root) for the log perpetual price, log spot price, and the log-basis <math id="A3.T4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{t}=\log F_{t}-\log S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{t}=\log F_{t}-\log S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>: levels are <math id="A3.T4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(1)</annotation></semantics></math> while the basis is stationary. “EG slope <math id="A3.T4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>” is the slope from the Engle-Granger regression <math id="A3.T4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log F_{t}=\alpha+\beta\log S_{t}+u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log F_{t}=\alpha+\beta\log S_{t}+u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>; the residual ADF rejects at any conventional level for all coins. “Half-life” is the implied half-life of a basis shock from a VECM with one lagged difference.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="A3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The Engle-Granger residual test and the Johansen trace test both reject the no-cointegration null at any conventional level. The estimated cointegrating slope is essentially one, and a VECM implies a basis half-life of about two hours for the larger coins and up to roughly <math id="A3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9.5</annotation></semantics></math> hours for DOGE, the natural empirical measure of the random horizon at which an RMA trade closes.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We also implement a purely statistical strategy that uses <em id="A3.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">only</em> the two price series. Each hour we form the standardized basis <math id="A3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}=u_{t}/\sigma_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}=u_{t}/\sigma_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> from a 30-day rolling cointegrating regression, open a position when <math id="A3.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|z_{t}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|z_{t}|</annotation></semantics></math> exceeds an entry threshold of <math id="A3.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.96</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.96</annotation></semantics></math> (shorting the perpetual and longing the spot when <math id="A3.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is high, and vice versa), and flatten when <math id="A3.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> reverts through zero. Table <a href="#A3.T5" title="Table C.5 ‣ C.2 Statistical Arbitrage with Cointegration ‣ Appendix C Alternative Arbitrage Strategies ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.5</span></a> compares it to the theory-motivated and data-driven RMA strategies under the no-trading-cost tier.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table C.5: </span>Statistical Arbitrage versus Random-maturity Arbitrage</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="A3.T5.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="A3.T5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Annualized Sharpe ratios and time-in-market for three strategies under the no-trading-cost tier and the DeFi risk-free rate. “StatArb” trades the standardized residual of a 30-day rolling cointegrating regression with no structural input; “RMA-theory” is the theory-motivated strategy of Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, and “RMA-data” the data-driven strategy of Appendix <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Appendix C Alternative Arbitrage Strategies ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>. Because the strategies are active for different fractions of the sample (“Active %”), Sharpe ratios are annualized following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lucca and Moench (2015)</a></cite>: active-subsample moments are scaled by the average number of active hours per year.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="A3.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The statistical strategy is profitable on every coin using no structural input, confirming that the cointegrating relation alone is exploitable; the structural strategies nonetheless dominate, because they stay in the market far more of the time and so harvest the smaller, persistent funding-driven deviations that the residual rule discards as noise.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Additional Empirical Results</h2>

<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Robustness to Alternative Risk-free Rate Measures</h3>

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show robustness in the random-maturity arbitrage strategies’ performance by considering alternative risk-free rates and present the results in Table <a href="#A4.T1" title="Table D.1 ‣ D.1 Robustness to Alternative Risk-free Rate Measures ‣ Appendix D Additional Empirical Results ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>. We conduct our analysis using daily T-bill rates sourced from Kenneth French’s data library (<a href="https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/f-f_factors.html" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/f-f_factors.html</a>) and margin interest rates from Binance (<a href="https://binance-docs.github.io/apidocs/spot/en/#query-margin-interest-rate-history-user_data" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://binance-docs.github.io/apidocs/spot/en/#query-margin-interest-rate-history-user_data</a>). We find that the performance of the trading strategy is robust to these alternative risk-free rates and across different trading costs tiers.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<table id="A4.T1.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>Deviations plus the Interest Rate</h3>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The deviation <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> in Equation (<a href="#S4.E17" title="In 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>) incorporates the interest rate <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>. To verify that the variation in <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is driven by futures prices rather than by variation in the interest rate, we add <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> back and examine</p>

<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3 </span>Portfolio Margin Event Study</h3>

<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To complement the portfolio-margin analysis in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, Figure <a href="#A4.F2" title="Figure D.2 ‣ D.3 Portfolio Margin Event Study ‣ Appendix D Additional Empirical Results ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a> plots futures-spot deviations around Binance’s introduction of portfolio margin on April 20, 2022. As discussed in the main text, portfolio margin allows gains and losses on spot and futures positions to be netted within a unified account, reducing the capital required to maintain the arbitrage trade.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v7/figures/pm_event_timeseries_upper_90d.png" id="A4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/176;" width="476" height="176" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure D.2: </span>Deviations of Perpetual Futures from No-arbitrage Benchmarks around the Introduction of Portfolio Margin</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="A4.F2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="A4.F2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents the 7-day moving averages of the annualized deviation of the perpetual futures from the no-arbitrage benchmark for five cryptocurrencies around the introduction of the Binance portfolio margin program with an event window of 90 trading days.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A4.F2" title="Figure D.2 ‣ D.3 Portfolio Margin Event Study ‣ Appendix D Additional Empirical Results ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a> shows that deviations are sizable and volatile before the introduction of portfolio margin and become visibly smaller afterward. This pattern is consistent across the five cryptocurrencies and provides a visual counterpart to the statistical evidence reported in Table <a href="#S5.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 5.3 Prediction 1: Arbitrage Constraints and Equilibrium Deviations ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> in the main text.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Together, the figure and the main-text estimates are consistent with Prediction 1: improving the capital efficiency of the arbitrage trade allows arbitrageurs to absorb larger positions and compresses deviations from the no-arbitrage benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.4 </span>Distribution of the Time to Payoff Realization</h3>

<div id="A4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each round trip of the theory-motivated random-maturity arbitrage strategy is one realization of the random unwinding time <math id="A4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> of Definition <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Definition 3 (Random-maturity arbitrage). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the time at which the arbitrage payoff is realized. Table <a href="#A4.T2" title="Table D.2 ‣ D.4 Distribution of the Time to Payoff Realization ‣ Appendix D Additional Empirical Results ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a> reports the distribution of these holding periods, in hours, at the zero-fee and the high-fee tier. We find that for a trader who pays no fees, the median holding period is two hours, and 98% of trades are closed within one day. For a trader who pays the highest fees, the median holding period is 38 hours (longest for BTC), and 90% of trades are closed within 10 days (224 hours).</p>
</div>

<section id="A4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.5 </span>Forward-looking Volatility</h3>

<div id="A4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ 5.1 Exploratory Evidence ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> measures arbitrageur risk using trailing 120-day realized volatility. Because this measure is backward-looking, we construct an ex ante HAR-RV forecast of realized volatility over the subsequent 120 days. Specifically, we regress future 120-day realized volatility on daily, weekly, and monthly lagged realized volatility and use the fitted value as the expected-volatility measure. The forecast uses only information available at the forecast date and is available for all five currencies over essentially the full sample.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A4.T3" title="Table D.3 ‣ D.5 Forward-looking Volatility ‣ Appendix D Additional Empirical Results ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a> shows that the results are similar to those in Table <a href="#S5.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ 5.1 Exploratory Evidence ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>. Expected volatility enters negatively and significantly for both <math id="A4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A4.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math>. The time trend remains negative and significant, while past returns remain positively associated with deviations. Thus, replacing backward-looking realized volatility with an ex ante forecast does not provide support for the simple prediction that higher expected volatility tightens arbitrageurs’ risk constraints and widens deviations.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.6 </span>Perpetual Order Flow and the Deviation</h3>

<div id="A4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If deviations from the no-arbitrage benchmark induce convergence trading, liquidity-demanding order flow in the perpetual market should lean against the deviation. In particular, when the perpetual is expensive relative to the benchmark, selling pressure in the perpetual market should increase. We examine this prediction using hourly signed taker order imbalance on Binance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Since every trade has a taker and a maker, we use the taker side to sign
each trade. Define hourly signed taker order imbalance in the perpetual
market as</p>
<table id="A4.E27" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<p id="A4.SS6.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A4.SS6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V^{perp,\text{taker buy}}_{i,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>taker buy</mtext></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{perp,\text{taker buy}}_{i,t}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="A4.SS6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V^{perp,\text{taker sell}}_{i,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mtext>taker sell</mtext></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{perp,\text{taker sell}}_{i,t}</annotation></semantics></math> denote dollar volume initiated by
taker buys, and taker sells, respectively, for currency <math id="A4.SS6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> in hour <math id="A4.SS6.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.
A higher value of <math id="A4.SS6.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="OIB^{perp}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">OIB^{perp}</annotation></semantics></math> therefore indicates greater
liquidity-demanding buying pressure, while a lower value indicates
greater selling pressure.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A4.T4" title="Table D.4 ‣ D.6 Perpetual Order Flow and the Deviation ‣ Appendix D Additional Empirical Results ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4</span></a> strongly supports the prediction. A one-unit increase
in the annualized deviation, roughly one and a quarter standard deviations,
lowers perpetual taker order imbalance by <math id="A4.SS6.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.1</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points, with a
<math id="A4.SS6.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>-statistic of <math id="A4.SS6.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-13.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>13.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-13.3</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, as perpetual futures become more expensive
relative to their no-arbitrage benchmark, liquidity-demanding order flow
shifts significantly toward selling the perpetual. This evidence is
consistent with market participants trading against deviations and exerting
price-convergence pressure.</p>
</div>

<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Proofs</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide proofs to Proposition <a href="#Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price: General Case). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, Proposition <a href="#Thmproposition2" title="Proposition 2 (No-arbitrage price: Edge Case). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, Corollary <a href="#Thmcorollary2" title="Corollary 2 (No-arbitrage price for Binance). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, and Proposition <a href="#Thmproposition3" title="Proposition 3 (No-arbitrage bounds with trading costs). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<p id="A5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proof to Proposition <a href="#Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price: General Case). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>:</span></p>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(30)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.p3.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p3.4.1" class="ltx_text">Because <math id="A5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(R)=1-R^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(R)=1-R^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> is strictly increasing in <math id="A5.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A5.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math> is weakly increasing with <math id="A5.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi^{-1}(r)=\{x^{*}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi^{-1}(r)=\{x^{*}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, we have</span></p>
<table id="A5.E31" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E31.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}&gt;0\Longleftrightarrow R_{t}&gt;\lambda\Longleftrightarrow p_{t}&gt;x^{*}\Longleftrightarrow\Phi(p_{t})&gt;r," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">⟺</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟺</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟺</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}&gt;0\Longleftrightarrow R_{t}&gt;\lambda\Longleftrightarrow p_{t}&gt;x^{*}\Longleftrightarrow\Phi(p_{t})&gt;r,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(31)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.p3.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p3.5.1" class="ltx_text">and all inequalities reverse when <math id="A5.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus the funding mechanism rewards the appropriate convergence trade on either side of the benchmark: if the perpetual is expensive relative to <math id="A5.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda S</annotation></semantics></math>, long <math id="A5.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> units of spot and short one perpetual; if it is cheap, reverse the trade.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sufficiency.</span>
Suppose first that <math id="A5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}=\lambda S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}=\lambda S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="A5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. Then <math id="A5.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t}=x^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t}=x^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(p_{t})=r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(p_{t})=r</annotation></semantics></math>. The gains on one long perpetual are therefore</p>
<table id="A5.E32" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E32.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="dF_{t}-\Phi(p_{t})F_{t}\,dt=\lambda\bigl(dS_{t}-rS_{t}\,dt\bigr)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dF_{t}-\Phi(p_{t})F_{t}\,dt=\lambda\bigl(dS_{t}-rS_{t}\,dt\bigr),</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="A5.p4.2" class="ltx_p">which are exactly the gains on <math id="A5.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> units of spot financed at the risk-free rate. The perpetual is therefore redundant given the spot and cash markets. Since the spot and cash markets admit no arbitrage, adding the perpetual cannot create a random-maturity arbitrage.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Necessity.</span>
We now show that any deviation from <math id="A5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=\lambda S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=\lambda S</annotation></semantics></math> generates a bounded-horizon random-maturity arbitrage. We begin with <math id="A5.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{0}&gt;\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{0}&gt;\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text">For one unit of the convergence trade, long <math id="A5.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> spot and short one perpetual, the discounted payoff from initiation to liquidation at time <math id="A5.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is</span></p>

</table>
<p id="A5.p6.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p6.2.1" class="ltx_text">The three terms have a direct interpretation. The first is the initial deviation captured by entering the convergence trade. The last is the cumulative funding received in excess of the financing cost of the spot leg. The middle term, <math id="A5.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-e^{-rt}u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-e^{-rt}u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, is the discounted cost of unwinding while a deviation remains. Unlike a fixed-maturity futures contract, a perpetual has no expiration date at which this last term is mechanically zero.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text">When <math id="A5.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, define the <em id="A5.p7.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">restoring rate</em></span></p>
<table id="A5.E34" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E34.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}\equiv\frac{[\Phi(p_{t})-r]F_{t}}{u_{t}}=\frac{R_{t}}{R_{t}-\lambda}\left[\Phi\!\left(1-\frac{1}{R_{t}}\right)-r\right]&gt;0." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≡</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}\equiv\frac{[\Phi(p_{t})-r]F_{t}}{u_{t}}=\frac{R_{t}}{R_{t}-\lambda}\left[\Phi\!\left(1-\frac{1}{R_{t}}\right)-r\right]&gt;0.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="A5.p7.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p7.2.1" class="ltx_text">The restoring rate is the net carry earned by the convergence trade per unit of the current deviation. It therefore has units of a rate: if the deviation and <math id="A5.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> were held fixed, the excess funding flow would earn back an amount equal to the current deviation in approximately <math id="A5.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> units of time. We call <math id="A5.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> a restoring rate because it measures the strength of the contract’s funding mechanism against a deviation. Importantly, it is not an assumption that <math id="A5.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> itself has a mean-reverting drift.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text">This interpretation suggests scaling down the convergence position as the excess carry accumulates. Define</span></p>

</table>
<p id="A5.p8.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p8.2.1" class="ltx_text">for as long as <math id="A5.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, and dynamically hold <math id="A5.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> units of the convergence trade. Because the perpetual position can be resized at zero entry cost and changes in the spot leg are offset in the cash account, this rebalancing is self-financing. Its discounted payoff is</span></p>
<table id="A5.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<p id="A5.p9.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p9.2.1" class="ltx_text">Here <math id="A5.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous and of finite variation, so <math id="A5.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[G,u]_{t}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[G,u]_{t}=0</annotation></semantics></math>. Moreover, <math id="A5.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="dG_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dG_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> is absolutely continuous with respect to <math id="A5.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds</annotation></semantics></math> and therefore assigns zero weight to individual jump times; hence <math id="A5.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{s-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>−</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{s-}</annotation></semantics></math> can be replaced by <math id="A5.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> in the <math id="A5.p9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="dG_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dG_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> integral.                 <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">16</span>
                
                
                
              See, e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Protter, 2012</a>)</cite> for the integration-by-parts formula for càdlàg semimartingales. Funding is a time-flow, <math id="footnote16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(p_{t})F_{t}dt" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(p_{t})F_{t}dt</annotation></semantics></math>, so a jump in prices changes the contemporaneous premium and subsequent funding rate but does not itself generate a lump-sum funding payment.</span></span></span></span></p>

<p id="A5.p13.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p13.4.1" class="ltx_text">The strategy has zero initial cost, is self-financing, and delivers a strictly positive payoff on every path no later than the deterministic time <math id="A5.p13.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>. It is therefore a random-maturity arbitrage.</span></p>

<div id="A5.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p15.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p15.1.1" class="ltx_text">We have shown that absence of random-maturity arbitrage requires <math id="A5.p15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{0}=\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{0}=\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>. Because the same argument can be initiated after resetting the clock at any date, it follows that <math id="A5.p15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{t}=\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{t}=\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="A5.p15.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore</span></p>
<table id="A5.E59" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

<p id="A5.p15.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p15.2.1" class="ltx_text">which proves necessity and completes the proof.

risk-free rate. Thus the perpetual is redundant given the spot and cash
markets, and the sufficiency argument of Proposition 1 implies that no
random-maturity arbitrage exists.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p24" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p24.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p24.1.1" class="ltx_text">Economically, this explains why the benchmark is an interval rather than
a point. Inside
<math id="A5.p24.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\underline{\lambda},\overline{\lambda}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><munder accentunder="true"><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\underline{\lambda},\overline{\lambda}]</annotation></semantics></math>, the funding rate equals the
financing rate exactly, so the excess carry and hence the restoring rate
are zero. Arbitrage therefore rules out prices outside the interval but
does not select a unique point within it.
∎</span></p>
</div>

<div id="A5.4" class="ltx_proof">

<p id="A5.p26.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p26.1.1" class="ltx_text">Write <math id="A5.p26.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=(F-S)/F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=(F-S)/F</annotation></semantics></math> for the premium index. Substituting the definition of the
clamp into the Binance funding rule gives</span></p>
<table id="A5.Ex47" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.Ex47.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(p)=\begin{cases}\kappa p+\gamma,&amp;\kappa p&lt;\iota-\gamma,\\[3.0pt]
\iota,&amp;\iota-\gamma\leq\kappa p\leq\iota+\gamma,\\[3.0pt]

</table>
<p id="A5.p26.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p26.2.1" class="ltx_text">The three branches agree at the two boundaries, so <math id="A5.p26.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous.
It is also weakly increasing, with slope <math id="A5.p26.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> outside the clamp and
slope zero inside it.</span></p>
</div>

</div>

</div>
<div id="A5.p31" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p31.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p31.1.1" class="ltx_text">Thus, on the linear branch containing the benchmark, excess funding is
exactly proportional to the price deviation. Economically, this is why
the restoring rate is constant there: doubling the deviation doubles the
excess funding flow.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p32" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p32.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p32.1.1" class="ltx_text">For completeness, when the premium lies inside the clamp,
<math id="A5.p32.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi(p_{t})=\iota" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>ι</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi(p_{t})=\iota</annotation></semantics></math>. Since</span></p>

</table>
<p id="A5.p32.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p32.3.1" class="ltx_text">Unlike on the linear branch, the funding flow inside the clamp is fixed
as a fraction of notional rather than proportional to the deviation, so
the restoring rate falls as the deviation becomes larger.
∎</span></p>
</div>

<p id="A5.p38.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p38.8.1" class="ltx_text">Thus the strategy earns strictly more than <math id="A5.p38.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> before trading costs.
Because the total discounted trading cost is bounded above by <math id="A5.p38.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, the
net payoff is strictly positive on <math id="A5.p38.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>. The strategy does nothing on
<math id="A5.p38.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>c</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{c}</annotation></semantics></math>, has nonpositive initial cost, and is liquidated by a deterministic
finite horizon. Hence it is a random-maturity arbitrage, a contradiction.
Therefore</span></p>

<p id="A5.p40.10" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p40.10.1" class="ltx_text">which proves the proposition.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p41" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p41.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.p41.1.1" class="ltx_text">For the Binance funding-rate specification, substituting the endpoints of <math id="A5.p41.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi^{-1}(r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi^{-1}(r)</annotation></semantics></math> derived in Corollary <a href="#Thmcorollary2" title="Corollary 2 (No-arbitrage price for Binance). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> gives Equations (<a href="#S3.E11" title="In 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>) and (<a href="#S3.E12" title="In 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>).</span></p>
